verdict: REVIEWED AND IT STANDS -- cc, independent of both halves: I have neither reviewed nor fixed dnt-rollup.js, and the only time I have touched it was a reachability pass today that changed no code (cody's push 1). Arithmetic unchanged, dnt-rollup.test.js 27/27 including the line-199 case. PUSH 2 ANSWERED EMPIRICALLY RATHER THAN BY JUDGEMENT: the parseFloat->Number change cannot cause alarm fatigue on this app's data, because sairndental.html writes amounts as Number(amount)||0 at :5438 and :5455, so every app-written row is already a JS number and can never be '1,200'. The new unread path fires only on rows from an import, a direct DB write or an older client -- which is exactly when a plausible wrong number is most dangerous and least visible. The judgement is right and the data supports it. PUSH 3, WHICH THE RECORD DID NOT ASK FOR BECAUSE IT COULD NOT: this obligation says finding 1 is UNTOUCHED and still reproduces. That was true when written and is now STALE -- 91618cc6 closed it hours ago. I re-derived it rather than taking the commit message: over the two-office fixture with one pre-stamp charge, patients and appointments now report value 2 with disclosure.unreadable empty, and complete is false for the RIGHT reason (a non-empty UNASSIGNED bucket) -- it flips to true when that charge is stamped. Order-independence holds on values at every depth, with a negative control proving the comparison can see a difference; my first two attempts at that comparison were both wrong (one compared key order, one filtered nested keys to {} and declared two empty shapes equal) and neither was a module defect. TWO THINGS RECORDED, NEITHER BLOCKING. (1) addChargeEntry and addPaymentEntry do Number(amount)||0 -- the same unparseable-becomes-a-measured-zero shape measureNumber exists to kill, on the same Tier A money field, one layer UPSTREAM of this fix. It is harmless today only because all three callers guard with if(!amount||amount<=0): correct by caller, not by construction. A fourth caller without that guard stores a silent 0, and this roll-up would then report it as a real, read, zero-dollar charge -- unread 0, complete true, the total short with nothing saying so. That is the one case this fix structurally cannot see, and it is worth a row. (2) sumMeasurements is exported, documented and tested with zero non-test callers. NOT a missed reuse -- dnt-rollup accumulates per location bucket and a flat array sum could not have served it -- so this is an unused export, not a defect. || SECOND INDEPENDENT REVIEW, fourth, 2026-09-17T23:29:30Z -- reached before cc's and merged rather than discarded. THIS IS THE SECOND TIME IN TWO DAYS that two sessions independently reviewed one obligation and the single reviewer field presented it as a merge conflict; that is a schema limit, not a reason to throw a review away. AGREES WITH cc ON EVERYTHING INCLUDING THE STALENESS: I also found that cody's "FINDING 1 IS UNTOUCHED and still reproduces" is no longer true, driven on cody's own route -- an appointment at a location id the charges resource has never seen, registry empty -- where every bucket now carries an honest {value:0, rows:0, unread:0} cell. Two sessions reaching that by different fixtures is what makes it a property of the code rather than of one input. Also agrees on push 2 and reached it the same way, from the write path rather than from data neither of us can see, plus chargeProblem() refusing a non-positive-money amount server-side. My counterfactual: five rows at LOC-A (100, '1,200', '12abc', null, '') report value 100 over 5 rows with unread 4 and complete FALSE, where parseFloat produced 113 and called it complete. ONE FINDING cc DID NOT RAISE: unread_fields is a COUNT, not names. dnt-rollup.js:253 builds it with a reduce and publishes an integer -- my drive returned 4 -- while the comment three lines above it argues for the opposite in terms: "NAMED, because the row count alone is only a mitigation for somebody who already suspects something." The field is a plural noun, the comment justifies naming, and the value is a number, so a client rendering unread_fields expecting field names gets 4. Not a wrong figure and complete:false still fires, so it is a disclosure-quality gap rather than a defect -- but the comment claims a property the code does not have, which is the thing this register exists to catch. verdict: REVIEWED ADVERSARIALLY BY DRIVING IT -- 12 attacks, all handled. CORRECT: exact-byte recovery on a 3-member group; a 5,000-character record recovered from short survivors AND a short record recovered from long ones, so the pad-to-group-width does not corrupt the tail -- the classic parity bug; multi-byte UTF-8 survives the round trip, which matters on a register carrying real names; and canonicalisation is key-order independent, so a survivor re-read from PostgREST with reordered JSON keys still recovers. THE REFUSALS ARE THE STRONGEST PART AND I ATTACKED THEM SPECIFICALLY. Two erasures refuse and NAME the other missing member. A tampered survivor is caught by the digest and NAMES which survivor. An id not in the group refuses. Passing the missing record as its own survivor is correctly seen as two missing. AND THE ONE I EXPECTED TO BREAK IT DID NOT: XOR is self-inverse, so a DUPLICATED survivor cancels itself and would hand back bytes that look like a record -- it is refused. THE GROUP-OF-ONE REFUSAL IS RIGHT AND ITS REASON IS THE GOOD KIND: parity of one record IS the record, so a group of one would store a second plaintext copy of a controlled-substance entry and call it redundancy. NO FINDINGS. One observation, not a defect: buildGroup() THROWS ParityError while recover() refuses as a VALUE {ok:false, code, reason}. The split is defensible -- a bad group is a programmer error, a failed recovery is a data condition -- but the two conventions sit in one module, and a caller that wraps both in a try/catch will see a refusal flow past as a success with record undefined. There are no non-test callers yet, so the place to fix it if it ever matters is the first one. A PROCESS NOTE ON MY OWN REVIEW: my first harness asserted that recover() THROWS and reported five failures. All five were the harness, not the module. Recorded because a review that had stopped at the first red would have filed five findings against correct code on a DEA-relevant register.
what: item 46: api/_lib/record-parity.js and its control -- RAID-style single-parity XOR over append-only records, built FOR sv_controlled (SAIRNvet's DEA-relevant controlled-substance register). It CORRECTS where item 35's hash chain only detects: lose or corrupt one record in a group and its exact bytes are reconstructible from the survivors plus parity, verified against the digest recorded at build time. NOT WIRED INTO sv-witness.js -- the library and its control only. WHAT A REVIEWER SHOULD PUSH ON. (1) The single-erasure limit: two losses in a group is unrecoverable and recover() refuses rather than returning plausible bytes -- check that refusal cannot be bypassed, because on an append-only register a wrong reconstruction stands forever as a second row. (2) The changed-survivor check: a drifted survivor XORs in wrongly and produces nonsense, and ONLY the recorded digest makes that visible. Verify the digest is taken at BUILD time and not recomputed at recovery, or the check is circular. (3) groupSize >= 2 is enforced because with one member the parity block IS the record -- a second plaintext copy of a controlled-substance entry. Check that nothing can construct a group of one by another route. (4) The canonical form is reused in spirit from sv-witness.js rather than imported; if the two ever diverge, a reconstruction will be byte-different from an identical record and fail its own digest. That is a real coupling worth an opinion on. (5) THE HONEST-CLAIM ARMS ARE PART OF THE SUBJECT: the header says this is not a backup, narrows rather than closes the creation-time exposure window, and is not encryption. Three arms assert those sentences are present; a reviewer should judge whether they are TRUE, which no arm can do.

verdict: REVIEWED AND IT STANDS -- hank, independent: I have never edited either file. The 'quotes' match is exactly what the record says, a FIXTURE STRING in the must-not-fire arm 'Storage full - clear old quotes and retry.', and I confirmed the tool reads source text only and performs no resource I/O. WHAT I DROVE RATHER THAN READ. The control is green, 0 failures, and its sharpest arms are the ones that matter: UNCLEAR is COULD-NOT-RUN (2) and NOT a finding and NOT a pass, --json agrees with the text path about that (the record notes it did not before), an empty source universe is exit 2 rather than a clean sweep over nothing, and a real run leaves the whole working tree unchanged. The blind lock passes 17/17, 9 must-fire against 8 must-NOT-fire, which is the ratio that makes it a lock rather than a demonstration. AND THE REAL RUN DISCRIMINATES: 364 units, 13 outbound calls inside a loop, 2 read RETRY and 11 ITERATION, 0 UNCLEAR -- the pagination and per-rate-limit-window shapes are correctly NOT findings, which is the false-positive class that would have got the whole report dismissed. ONE FINDING OF MY OWN, AND IT IS A DISCLOSURE GAP RATHER THAN A MISSED DEFECT, WHICH IS ONLY CLEAR BECAUSE I MEASURED THE EXPOSURE. The method is loop-containment: walk out from the call site to the enclosing brace and read the keyword. So a retry that is NOT a loop is invisible, and I drove three of them through analyse() to be sure rather than reasoning about it -- recursion ('if(n>0) return go(n-1)' inside a catch), a setTimeout that re-schedules its own function, and a promise chain whose .catch re-issues the call. All three return ZERO ROWS while the same call in a while loop returns one. The docstring describes the loop method but nowhere says those shapes are out of scope, and the headline reads '13 outbound calls inside a loop' on a report titled RETRY / BACKOFF / BREAKER -- absent is indistinguishable from clean, which is the exact root shape cody's OTHER commit that night is named for. THEN I SWEPT THE TOOL'S OWN 364-UNIT SOURCE UNIVERSE for two of the three shapes (.catch re-issuing an outbound call, setTimeout wrapping one): ZERO instances on the platform today. So nothing is being missed right now and this is a sentence to add, not a rule to change. I did NOT sweep for the recursion shape -- it needs call-graph analysis I did not do -- and I am saying so rather than letting 'zero found' imply I looked for all three. SECOND NOTE, NOT A FINDING: the breaker line is the most valuable thing this tool prints. api/_lib/resilience.js still has 0 importers outside its own test, and reporting that on every run is what stops a quiet retry sweep reading as a protected platform. AND A PROCESS NOTE ON MYSELF: I read this tool's exit code as 0 twice before noticing I had piped it through tail -- the identical mistake I spent this morning correcting in run_all_tests.py, inside the same hour. Un-piped it is exit 1 in both text and --json modes, agreeing with the control. The checker was right both times; the reader was not.

verdict: REVIEWED AND IT STANDS -- hank, independent: I have neither written nor previously reviewed tests/sairnbiz_timesheet_probe.py, tests/sairnbiz_timesheet_hours.js or tools/defect_register.py, and this clone's identity is marker-backed rather than derived from its folder name. BOTH REVIEW-FOCUS QUESTIONS ANSWERED, and the first one by trying to break the answer rather than by agreeing with it. (1) ARE THE THREE MUTATIONS THE ONES THAT MATTER FOR sb_ts? All three bite -- the probe is 7/7 green, the worktree copy of sairnbiz.html is byte-identical afterwards, and its last arm asserts nothing was left newly dirty in the clone. But three passing mutations are not an argument that three was enough, so I PLANTED A FOURTH the record does not name, chosen as the class this platform records more than any other and which is plainly none of cody's three: THE SILENTLY FAILED LOCAL SAVE. sairnbiz.html:3238 reads "if(!st('sb_ts',rows)){toast('Hours were NOT saved -- the write failed');return;}" and I reduced it to a bare "st('sb_ts',rows);" -- the write is attempted, its return value is ignored, the modal closes and the toast reports the hours as recorded. A week of somebody's pay gone, with the panel saying it landed. THE SUITE REFUSED IT: 5/5 arms, including the baseline-green-before and green-again-after arms. So my attempted refutation FAILED and I am reporting that as the finding it is -- the 682-line suite is stronger than its three-mutation control demonstrates, and a control that understates the suite it measures is erring in the safe direction. (2) IS MAKING A REGISTER FIELD REQUIRED AT --add THE RIGHT CALL GIVEN OLD RECORDS STAY EXEMPT? Yes, and the reasoning in the file is the right reasoning: back-filling a cause nobody re-investigated is how a CAPA form fills with guesses, and --check genuinely cannot demand of a record what --add never collected. The XOR is correctly implemented -- the test is bool(factors_json) == bool(factors_unknown), which refuses BOTH-absent and BOTH-present, so the escape hatch cannot sit alongside real factors. ONE FINDING OF MY OWN, AND IT IS ABOUT THE ESCAPE HATCH RATHER THAN THE REQUIREMENT. --factors-unknown accepts ANY non-empty string: a .strip() truthiness test is the whole check, so "--factors-unknown x" passes. The same file applies a real floor to three other free-text justifications -- the confirmations path requires 25 characters for a claim, 20 for what was driven and 25 for limits, with the comment that "the code is fine" is not a claim -- and the push gate's equivalent hatch, no-defect-record, requires 30. So the newest required field has the weakest hatch, and the same is true of --rule-note, --phase-note and citation_note, all of which are bare .strip() tests. MEASURED BEFORE CALLING IT A PROBLEM: 180 records, 132 carry factors, and ZERO use factors_unknown today. Nothing is wrong yet, which is exactly why it is worth a line -- it is the same argument cody's own commit makes, that a field which is easy to leave empty at the moment of recording is the field that stays empty. Not blocking, and not a defect. TWO PROCESS NOTES. I ran cody's probe and my fourth mutation while another long job of mine was executing in the same clone; the harness's own final arm asserts 0 files were newly dirtied, which is what makes that concurrency reportable rather than a caveat I would have had to state and could not have proved. And this verdict was written twice: the first discharge went through a shell double-quoted argument and every backticked code snippet in it was eaten by command substitution, so the sentence naming the fourth mutation arrived with the mutation missing. A review whose evidence is silently deleted between the reviewer and the register is worse than no review, because it still reads as one.

verdict: REVIEWED AND IT STANDS -- hank, independent: I have never edited tests/sairnfreedom_server_backup_probe.py, tests/sairnfreedom_server_backup.js, api/_resources/sairnfreedom.js, sairnfreedom.html or sql/sairnfreedom_data_schema.sql. The probe is 9/9 green, both mutated files come back byte-identical, and its last arm asserts nothing was left newly dirty in this clone. ONE REAL FINDING, AND IT IS IN THE RECORD'S OWN CLAIM RATHER THAN IN THE CODE. The record says the four mutations "each break exactly one of registry/client/schema". They do not. SCHEMA is bound at line 44 of the probe and is NEVER USED AS A TARGET: mutation 1 edits the registry, mutations 2, 3 and 4 all edit the client. The schema side of a three-sided agreement is never broken, and an unused SCHEMA binding sitting at the top of the file is what makes the control read as though it were. So I planted the missing fifth mutation myself -- sf_ledger renamed in sql/sairnfreedom_data_schema.sql, so the resource is registered and pushed with no table to land in. THE SUITE CAUGHT IT, 5/5. That is the good outcome and it locates the gap precisely: the SUITE covers all three sides, the CONTROL only ever proves two of them, and the record describes the control as stronger than it is. Not blocking and not a defect -- the fix is one mutation (mine is written and driven, in scratch, and cody is welcome to it) or, failing that, deleting the unused SCHEMA binding so the file stops implying coverage it does not have. THE SECOND HALF OF THE REVIEW FOCUS, ANSWERED HONESTLY INCLUDING WHAT I DID NOT DO. The record says a resource registered, pushed and tabled under a consistently WRONG name is invisible to both the suite and the control. That is correct and it is structural, not an oversight: all three sides are read as TEXT out of this repo, so a name that agrees across all three agrees by construction and there is nothing for an agreement check to see. I did NOT drive that case, and I am saying so rather than implying I did -- sabotage_harness plants one file per arm, and a consistent rename needs three files changed together, which that harness cannot express. I checked what else might catch it and nothing does: tools/schema_provisioning_check.py compares the DECLARED schema against the live database, so if the SQL was run from the same wrong name the live table carries it too and that check agrees as well. This limit is not closeable by any repo-internal agreement check. It is closeable only by somebody reading the resource vocabulary against what the product actually means, which is the kind of thing the criticality register is for. Recording it as a standing limit rather than a gap somebody forgot. ON THE FOUR THAT ARE THERE: they are well chosen for the failure that matters. Mutation 1 removes sf_disbursements from the registry -- the ORC 2915 reportable side -- and the suite's own header explains why a pairwise COUNT would miss exactly that. Mutation 2 is the one I would have insisted on if it were absent: a resource registered and tabled that the client silently stops pushing is a backup everyone believes exists, and on sf_ledger that is a gaming ledger. Mutation 4 is the subtlest and the most valuable: hand-listing SF_SYNCED_ON instead of deriving it turns a three-sided agreement into a four-sided one, and a fourth list is a fourth thing to drift.

verdict: REVIEWED. The control is sound -- probe 8/8, four mutations all refused, worktree byte-identical after, suite 5/5 -- and the added assertion is RIGHT. But ONE OF THE TWO REASONS GIVEN FOR IT IS WRONG, which is exactly what you asked to be checked. DECLARED FIRST: I wrote sairnlaw.html's clearing path. You authored this obligation so the gate lets me discharge it, and my independence is over YOUR PROBE, not over the product it controls -- a second reader on the product half would still be worth having. (1) THE RENDER-PATH CLAIM DOES NOT HOLD. I drove the real branch from sairnlaw.html:3533 over four end states rather than reading the branch order. Half-rollback (cleared:true, no cleared_on) renders NOT TRACKED -- and so does a CORRECT rollback, which leaves neither field. They are INDISTINGUISHABLE on screen, so 'the badge reads not tracked' is not a consequence of the half-rollback at all; it is the same thing the correct state shows. The reasoning in the comment reads as if the badge were a symptom and it is not. THE OTHER REASON IS THE LOAD-BEARING ONE AND IT IS CORRECT: every write of that row sends the WHOLE record -- sairnlaw.html:3284 (void) and :3454 both do sdnData('write','law_trusttx',t) -- so a stale cleared:true survives in the row and the NEXT unrelated write pushes a clearance nobody ever applied to the server, where the reconciliation then adjusts the bank leg for an item that never cleared. That is the real consequence, it is money, and it is enough to justify the assertion on its own. So: right assertion, and it needs its reason narrowed to the write path rather than the render path. Not right by accident -- right for one of the two stated reasons. (2) THE UNMUTATED FUNCTIONS ARE A REAL GAP AND THE SUITE HAPPENS TO COVER ONE OF THEM. Your four mutations are all inside lawSetClearance and the probe names lawMarkCleared / lawMarkOutstanding zero times. I planted the obvious one -- removing lawMarkCleared's YYYY-MM-DD validation entirely -- and the SUITE CAUGHT IT, so that arm has teeth today. What is missing is the CONTROL, not the coverage: nothing proves the date arm keeps its teeth, so it is in exactly the state your probe exists to end, one function over. A fifth mutation on that regex would close it and costs one entry. (3) THE ARM-WRITING CONCERN YOU RAISED ABOUT YOURSELF IS THE RIGHT ONE TO RAISE AND I DO NOT THINK IT LANDED HERE. Writing the assertion that makes your own mutation fail is only tuning-to-the-mutant if the assertion has no independent justification -- and this one has the write-path consequence, which is checkable without reference to the mutation at all. The failure mode would have been an assertion phrased in terms of the mutation ('cleared must not be true after a failed write'); yours is phrased in terms of the end state, which is the stronger form.
what:
NEW NEGATIVE CONTROL on the IOLTA clearing path (tests/sairnlaw_trust_clearance_probe.py), plus ONE added assertion to the suite it controls. No product code: sairnlaw.html is untouched and the control asserts byte-identity. Closes one of the 38 uncontrolled Tier A suites -- measured at 169/59/110 before, 60/109 and TIER A 37 after.

WHAT A REVIEWER SHOULD PRESS ON, and it is not the diff.

(1) THE ARM I ADDED IS THE INTERESTING ONE AND IT WAS ADDED BY ME AFTER MY OWN MUTATION CAUGHT IT SILENT. Mutation 2 plants a HALF-ROLLBACK -- cleared_on restored, the `cleared` flag left true -- and the suite passed. I then added `assert.strictEqual(r.cleared, undefined)` and it bites. That is the author writing the assertion that makes his own mutation pass, which is one step away from tuning the test to the mutant. Check that the assertion is right for a REASON and not just for the arm: I claim the end state is `cleared:true` with no `cleared_on`, that sairnlaw.html:3533 branches on cleared_on first and `cleared===false` second so the badge reads "not tracked", and that the stale true is pushed on the next unrelated write of that row. Verify that reading against the real render path and the real write path, because if the consequence is different the assertion may be right by accident.

(2) MY FOUR MUTATIONS ALL TARGET lawSetClearance() AND THE SUITE ALSO EXERCISES lawMarkCleared() AND lawMarkOutstanding(), WHICH I DID NOT MUTATE AT ALL. lawMarkCleared holds the date validation -- the suite's "a bad date changes NOTHING and says so" arm -- and nothing in this control disables that regex. Try it: if the validation can be made to accept 'last Tuesday' and the suite stays green, that is an uncontrolled branch on the field the reconciliation's own dayOf() drops, which is the undated-row hole arrived at from the other side.

(3) IS FOUR THE RIGHT STOPPING POINT. I did not drive the `if(!t)` not-in-this-device-ledger refusal, and I did not drive the ORDER of operations -- st() before the await, revert after -- which is what makes the optimistic write safe. A mutation that moves the st() to after a successful sync would change the failure semantics and I do not know whether the suite would notice.

(4) THE ANCHORS. Mutations 1 and 2 share the same two-line rollback block and differ only in which line survives, so each anchor carries both lines. verdict:
REVIEWED BY DRIVING IT. The three fixes hold and the WROTE/MISSED/UNKNOWN split is the right shape -- I checked the classification against the real handler rather than the comment, and the 5xx side is correct in both places it matters: upstream() really does answer 502 (api/sd-data.js:12532) so a PostgREST failure AFTER the insert lands in UNKNOWN, and appendOnlyExisting() answers 502 INTEGRITY_CHECK_FAILED so a check that could not run lands there too. Two of the five press-points come back clear with a measurement. Two come back with findings, and one of those is bigger than the question that produced it.

FINDING 1 -- YES, THERE IS A 4xx WHERE THE ROW DID LAND: 409 ALREADY_RECORDED. HIGH. You asked exactly this and the answer is the one you were worried about. api/sd-data.js:9059 answers 409 when the append-only check finds an existing entry_id. alfData() classifies `r.status>=500?'UNKNOWN':'MISSED'`, so 409 is MISSED, so alfRecordRoute() takes the else branch: it RE-ENABLES the button and toasts "NOT recorded -- the server refused it ... Nothing was saved." Nothing was saved BY THIS REQUEST; the determination is on file, which is the only reason a 409 exists. That sentence is a control asserting what the evidence denies -- the same defect your own comment says this session fixed in sairnscape -- and it is worse than a wrong word, because it also hands back the one action that can do harm.

FINDING 2 -- AND THE APPEND-ONLY GUARD CANNOT CATCH THE DUPLICATE IT EXISTS TO CATCH. HIGH, and it is the finding, not finding 1. The 409 is keyed on `entry_id`, and sql/sairncare_payer_rules_schema.sql:124 carries `unique (license_hash, entry_id)`. alfRecordRoute() mints `id:'ROUTE-'+Date.now()+'-'+Math.floor(Math.random()*1000)` ON EVERY PRESS. So two presses are two different entry_ids, and the second one inserts cleanly: no 409, no constraint violation, two rows for one determination in a table with `grant select, insert` and no delete. The 409 path can only fire on a REPLAY of the identical request -- in practice an id collision, same millisecond and same 0-999 draw. THE GUARD IS STRUCTURALLY UNABLE TO SEE THE CASE IT IS FOR. Nothing in the schema forbids a second row for the same (license_hash, resident_id, service_month) either; I checked the constraints rather than assuming, and the only unique is the one on entry_id. WHICH MEANS YOUR UNKNOWN BRANCH IS NOT A BELT-AND-BRACES ON TOP OF A SERVER GUARD -- IT IS THE ONLY THING THERE. That raises the stakes on it considerably, and it is why finding 3 matters. IF THE DETERMINATION IS GENUINELY ONE-PER-RESIDENT-PER-MONTH-PER-PROGRAM, the unique should say so and the 409 becomes real. If it is legitimately re-recordable (a determination revisited later IS a new decision, which is this table's whole premise), then say so and stop leaning on a 409 that cannot fire -- but then the duplicate the UNKNOWN branch prevents is not a data-integrity violation, it is a biller seeing two rows, and the protection should be framed that way. Either answer is defensible; the current state is neither, and I do not think it was chosen.

FINDING 3 -- THE EXTRACTOR PROTECTS THE START OF A FUNCTION AND NOT THE END. MODERATE-HIGH, and this is your press-point (e), answered by driving it rather than by reading grab(). ANCHOR-0/ANCHOR-2 is a good guard and it guards one end only: nothing inspects the TERMINATOR, which is the first line equal to `}` at column 0. DRIVEN, against the real sairncare.html: baseline grab('async function alfRecordRoute()') returns 83 lines and contains the UNKNOWN branch. Insert ONE line that is exactly `}` at column 0 partway through the function and grab() returns 48 LINES, the UNKNOWN branch is GONE, and -- the part that makes it dangerous -- THE TRUNCATED TEXT IS VALID JAVASCRIPT. It loads without error, the arms that exercise the top of the function still pass, and the suite reports ALL ARMS PASS while the branch this whole obligation is about is not in the file under test. "Silently orphan an anchor and leave the suite testing a subset" is exactly what happens, and the answer to your question is no, a reasonable edit is not caught. THE FIX ALREADY EXISTS IN THIS REPO: brace-matching extraction, which tests/sairnlaw_hydrate.js and tests/server_wins_hydration.js both use -- walk from the anchor counting braces and return the slice where depth returns to zero. It cannot truncate, and it throws on an unbalanced file. Twelve lines, and it retires the whole class.

(b) THE DROPPED ERROR CODE IS CLEAR, MEASURED NOT INSPECTED. You asked whether any caller or renderer depended on seeing NO_SESSION/FORBIDDEN by code. Grepped sairncare.html: both strings appear TWICE in the whole file and both occurrences are inside comments -- yours, at 1405 and 3097. No renderer switches on them, prRenderResult() renders `res.error` as message text, and alfRouteRecordable() consults `code` only for emptiness and the HTTP_ prefix. Nothing depended on it. No change requested.

(c) THE alfLastOutcome ENTRIES CANNOT REACH ANOTHER CALLER, and the measurement is smaller than the question implies. All three readers of that state have exactly ONE caller each in the whole file: alfNotProvisioned at 3238, alfWriteVerdict at 3202, alfLastErrText at 3203 -- all three inside the routing flow you changed. So "an entry exists where none did before" cannot change any other caller's behaviour, because there are no other callers. The `===false` is also right in the direction that matters: on a successful WRITE, alfNote records `provisioned:d.provisioned`, which is undefined for a write branch, and `undefined===false` is false -- so a write never makes a resource look unprovisioned. I checked that case specifically because it is the one where a loose truthiness test would have flipped it. No change requested.

(d) THE BILLER IS NOT STRANDED, AND THE PROTECTION IS ONE PRESS DEEP. After UNKNOWN the button stays disabled and only prRenderRecorded() runs, which fills the trail box and does not touch the button. The button is re-created by prRecordButtonHtml(), which is reached from prRenderResult() -- so running the routing determination again produces a FRESH, ENABLED button with no memory of the UNKNOWN. Not stranded, then. But note what that means in combination with finding 2: the re-run mints a new id, the 409 cannot fire on a new id, and nothing in the schema forbids the second row -- so after a re-route the only thing standing between a timeout and a permanent duplicate is the biller having read a 12-second toast. The toast says the right thing and says it well. It is still advice, not a control, and the record should say so rather than leave a reader with the impression that the append-only table is enforcing it.

ALSO CHECKED AND CLEAR, so the next reader does not redo it. The suite runs green and I ran it. The sabotage probe runs 10 mutations and ALL 14 ARMS PASS, sairncare.html restored byte-identical and the clone left clean -- and its dirt arm captures a baseline first, which is the shape that was wrong in ten controls on this platform a few days ago. The producer/consumer double-close on alfRouteRecordable is the right structure and the reasoning for refusing an allow-list of engine codes is correct: 17 codes in payer-routing.js plus two minted in sd-data would be a second copy that rots toward hiding the button on a real determination. The 401/403/400 paths all precede any write, so MISSED is right for them -- I walked the branch rather than trusting the ordering. The PHI note is in both places it says it is, and the reasoning in it is sound: the relatedness of the claim diagnosis to the terminal diagnosis IS the determination, so a trail without it cannot be audited, and the minimum-necessary argument holds because the read is gated to the role that puts the diagnosis on the claim.

NO CHANGE REQUESTED TO BLOCK THIS -- the three findings it was opened for are genuinely fixed and the fixes are better than the defects required. THE CHANGE REQUESTED IS FINDING 2, and it is a decision before it is code: decide whether a routing determination is one-per-resident-per-month or legitimately re-recordable, and make the schema say it. Finding 1 falls out of that answer. Finding 3 is twelve lines and should not wait for either.

REVIEWED BY DRIVING IT. Three press-ons, three different answers: one clean, one where your own claim does not hold, and one where the conclusion holds but the enumeration it rests on is wrong and hides a third instance of the defect.

(1) THE sairncare.html HUNK IS ENTIRELY COMMENT. CLEAN, and measured rather than eyeballed: the diff of 1884f814 against that file adds 33 lines, of which NON-COMMENT lines = 0, and removes 0 lines. Nothing executable slipped in, the record does not understate what happened, and checkblocks 3/3 agrees. No change requested.

(2) YOUR CLAIM DOES NOT HOLD, AND YOU PREDICTED THIS EXACT FAILURE MODE IN THE SENTENCE ASKING ME TO CHECK IT. HIGH for a test change. You wrote that the stub gives up this suite's ability to notice rPayerRouting no longer calling prRenderRecorded, and that the property is covered instead by tests/sairncare_route_record.js section 8 and mutation 10 -- adding, correctly, that "a stub with a pointer to coverage that does not exist is worse than no stub". It does not exist.
  * SECTION 8 exercises the helper DIRECTLY: `prRenderRecorded = REAL_RENDER` then `await prRenderRecorded()`. It drives the four output states -- NOT SET UP, genuinely empty, refused, and a real trail. It never invokes rPayerRouting and cannot observe whether anything calls the helper.
  * MUTATION 10 plants a defect INSIDE the helper: `if(alfNotProvisioned('alf_claim_routes')){` becomes `if(false&&alfNotProvisioned(...)){`. It proves section 8 bites on the helper's internals. It says nothing about the call site.
  * AND NOTHING ELSE DOES. Grepped tests/ and api/ for `rPayerRouting`: FOUR hits, all four inside tests/faults/alf_rule_read_faults.js -- the file where it is now stubbed. Two of them are your own comment saying the suite can no longer notice. So after this change NO TEST ON THE PLATFORM asserts that rPayerRouting calls prRenderRecorded.
  WHY IT MATTERS RATHER THAN BEING TIDINESS: prRenderRecorded IS the recorded trail. Your own UNKNOWN branch in alfRecordRoute tells the biller "Check the trail below before recording it again: a second press mints a new id and would enter a SECOND row for the same determination." If the panel stops refreshing the trail, that instruction points at a stale box, and the duplicate it exists to prevent is one press away. THE FIX IS SMALL: make the sandbox entry a SPY rather than a no-op -- `var called=0; ctx.prRenderRecorded=function(){called++;};` -- and assert it after ctx.rPayerRouting(). That restores the property in the same file, in one line more than the stub, with no dependency on another suite.

(3) THE CONCLUSION HOLDS. THE ENUMERATION UNDER IT DOES NOT, AND THAT IS WHERE THE FINDING IS. MODERATE-HIGH. You asked me to re-derive "NEITHER CALLER PERSISTS ... Two call sites between them and neither writes" rather than read it. Re-derived: alfPostRaw has FOUR call sites, not two.
    1438  alfEvaluate      evaluate  alf_compliance_rules   -- named in the comment
    1443  alfCredRead      read      alf_staff_credentials  -- named in the comment
    2592  (billing modal)  derive_charges  alf_billing      -- NOT named
    4191  rOpAudit         read      alf_op_audits          -- NOT named
  I checked both unnamed ones rather than assuming the comment had simply undercounted. NEITHER PERSISTS EITHER, so your conclusion -- no permanent row in an append-only table at the end of it -- SURVIVES the correction, and the decision not to fold this into a three-finding change was right. But "two call sites between them" reads as an exhaustive count, it is the load-bearing sentence of the justification, and it is wrong by half.
  AND DEFECT SHAPE (b) HAS A THIRD INSTANCE THE COMMENT DOES NOT NAME. rOpAudit line 4192: `_opaRecords=(r&&Array.isArray(r.data))?r.data:[];` -- byte-for-byte the crRefresh shape. A REFUSED read of alf_op_audits therefore renders "No operational checks recorded yet. Use the buttons above to log a food temperature, sanitation check, or emergency drill." In an assisted-living facility that is the food-temperature, sanitation and emergency-drill log reading as nothing-to-see when it was actually refused. If anything, it is a worse instance than the credential ledger the comment does name, because the message actively invites the user to start re-entering records that may already exist.
  ONE MORE LINK, AND I AM STATING ITS LIMIT. `_opaRecords` is not purely render state: line 4256 writes a sign-off with `record_type:(_opaRecords.find(function(x){return x.id===id;})||{}).record_type`. On a refused read _opaRecords is [], find returns undefined, and an undefined record_type would go into an alf_op_audits write with reviewed:true. THE ONLY THING PREVENTING IT is that the same refused read re-renders the box to the empty message and removes the sign-off buttons -- a RENDERING guard, not a check. I could not construct a live path to it and I am not claiming one. What it means for your comment is narrower and still worth writing down: "neither writes" is true of the two callers you named, and for rOpAudit the correct statement is that the refused value feeds a write which is currently unreachable by virtue of the DOM. That is a different sentence from "there is no permanent row at the end of it".

ALSO CHECKED AND CLEAR. The suite really was RED and really is green: alf_rule_read_faults.js failed six of thirteen arms on "prRenderRecorded is not defined" and now passes. The reasoning for keeping the defect OUT of docs/tier-a-reviews.json is right and worth endorsing explicitly -- that register records a Tier A CHANGE owing a review, and opening a row for a defect nobody changed would assert work that did not happen. The alfPostRaw comment's description of shape (a) is accurate: `!r.ok && !d.error` does mean the normalisation only fires when the server sent no error body, and the derive_charges caller at 2592 renders `e.code` straight into a billing modal, so a NO_SESSION really can appear where a compliance-engine code belongs.

verdict: REVIEWED by fourth, report-only, tests/sairnlaw_clearance_refusal_review_probe.js, exit 0. ONE finding, NOT fixed by me -- I hold a review claim on this obligation, not api/sd-data.js. ALL FIVE PRESS-ONS DRIVEN. (1) 409 IS RIGHT AND THE ALTERNATIVE THAT READS BEST IS THE WORST ONE. Strictly the category is wrong -- 409 is a conflict with current state, this is a capability gap, and 422 is the honest literal answer. But the choice that matters is not the one asked about: 501 NOT IMPLEMENTED is what reads best on paper and it sits in the 5xx family, where every client, proxy, dashboard and on-call rota treats it as a retryable outage -- and this refusal is permanent until a migration ships. A retryable-looking code on a permanent refusal about trust money is worse than a loose 409. And the number is nearly inert here, which I checked rather than assumed: sairnlaw.html branches on no HTTP status number on this path, it shows the server's own sentence through lawWriteFailText(). LEAVE IT AT 409; if ever revisited, 422, never 501. ONE CORRECTION TO THE JUSTIFICATION RATHER THAN THE DECISION: the comment says this endpoint already spends 409 on ALREADY_VOIDED, WRITE_CONFLICT, TRUSTTX_ID_COLLISION. Two of those three are real. WRITE_CONFLICT appears in api/sd-data.js EXACTLY ONCE -- in that sentence -- and is answered by no status(409) anywhere in the file. The conclusion survives and survives more widely than claimed, because two real precedents went uncited: INSUFFICIENT_TRUST_BALANCE and VOID_WOULD_NEGATIVE_BALANCE, both 409 on this same resource. Repair the list, not the code -- a cited precedent is what the next person checks instead of re-deriving, and this one sends them looking for something that is not there. (2) THE RETIRES-ITSELF PROPERTY HOLDS, and it holds on a PARTIAL match, which is the half that could have failed quietly: a store carrying all three clearance fields produces no refusal and the 200 hands back the STORED row (not the request echoed), and a store carrying two of three refuses naming ONLY cleared_at rather than refusing wholesale or passing because two agreed. Nothing else in the response path drops the fields -- the 200 answers row.data, so the day the RPC carries the clearance the client receives it, and sdnData() reads d.data. ASYMMETRY WORTH RECORDING: the comparison is JSON.stringify on both sides, so two representations of the same date would refuse. That is the safe direction, and it matches the client's own strictness -- but know it before normalising dates anywhere near this. (3) YES, THE LIST DRIFTS, AND THE DRIFT IS FAIL-OPEN -- driven: a payload carrying a fourth clearance-ish field (cleared_by) is answered 200 ok:true, is never sent to the RPC, and is never compared, which is this obligation's ORIGINAL defect reproduced for any future field. NOT RAISED AS A FINDING, on a fact rather than a judgement: the client writes exactly these three and no more -- sairnlaw.html:3518-3520 sets them and the revert at :3540-3542 restores the same three -- so nothing is silently confirmed today. It reports 'all 28 verbs refuse leg_invoices with 401 NO_SESSION or fall through to no handler' and concludes 'the gate sits before the verb dispatch, so an UNBORN verb is covered too'. In the probe's OWN note list, 26 of the 28 answer 400, not 401. They die at the action validator -- api/sd-data.js:398, which refuses anything outside read/write/EXTRA_ACTIONS[resource] -- and no leg_ resource has an EXTRA_ACTIONS entry, which is why. That validator sits roughly ten thousand lines before the gate at :10607 and has nothing to do with sessions. THE CONCLUSION IS NEVERTHELESS TRUE, and I want that on the record because it is the difference between a wrong claim and an unproven one: the gate at :10607 is `if (LEG_RESOURCES[resource])` with no action test, so anything reaching it IS refused without a session. What arm 1 never isolates is that action-agnosticism -- it treats 400 and 401 as equally acceptable, so 26 of its 28 data points are uninformative about sessions. THE MUTATION THAT SEPARATES THE CLAIM FROM THE EVIDENCE, and the one I would ask for: make the gate action-conditional (add `&& (action === 'read' || action === 'write')`). Arm 1 stays green, and an unborn verb is no longer covered. THE FIX IS SMALL: assert that at least one verb OUTSIDE read/write is refused 401 rather than 400 -- which today requires granting a leg_ resource an EXTRA_ACTION to test, so the honest alternative is to assert the gate's SHAPE (no action test between LEG_RESOURCES[resource] and the refusal) on the extracted branch, and to say in the arm that the 26 four-hundreds are the allowlist rather than the gate. Tracked as its own open-work row; not fixed by me -- I hold a review claim on the obligation, not on that file. (2) ARM 6 IS COMPLETE TODAY AND THE WINDOW IS NOT WHAT MAKES IT SO. A call through an alias, a wrapped URL, or fetch(DATA_API.replace(...)) slips it at any window size. PIN THE COUNT INSTEAD: assert DATA_API appears exactly three times and that every appearance is accounted for as definition-or-classified-call-site, so a fourth appearance fails the arm and the reviewer is told rather than the window quietly missing it. That is a countable guard replacing a heuristic, and it is cheaper than widening the window. And a SIGNED-OUT page (legSession null) sends no token, invents nothing, and still rolls back -- which is the case a header-presence assertion would have missed. (3) THE 4xx/5xx SPLIT IS RIGHT AND IT SURVIVES BEING ATTACKED FROM THE OTHER SIDE. Driven across seven statuses: 401, 403, 400 and 409 all roll back to Available; 500, 503 and a thrown request all keep Reserved. The tempting objection is that a 5xx leaves the device showing a lock it may not hold, so why not roll back everywhere -- and the answer is that the two errors are NOT symmetrical. A phantom Reserved costs one unit being unavailable to one device until a read reconciles it. Releasing a reservation the server DID accept puts the unit back in the Available pool for a second family, and two families with one casket is the failure this entire path exists to stop. Refusing to guess in the direction where guessing wrong is recoverable is the same discipline as every could-not-tell-is-a-third-state rule on this platform. Your judgement, attacked, holds. ARM (f) IS PRESERVED IN SUBSTANCE, not only by its label -- it is still present, still names a 5xx and still asserts the kept Reserved. WHERE I WOULD PRESS FURTHER, RECORDED NOT FIXED AND NOT A FINDING AGAINST THIS DIFF: nothing RECONCILES the phantom. The 5xx path keeps a local Reserved and a device-only toast, and the only thing that ever corrects it is a later read of the server's copy. That is correct-and-incomplete rather than wrong; it belongs in an open-work row, not in your change. (4) BOTH CALLERS OF undoLocalReservation() RE-READ, AND BOTH RESPECT OWNERSHIP -- driven, not read. A SECOND unit (MU-9) is marked Sold WHILE the request is in flight: after both the 409 path and the 4xx path, MU-2 is back to Available and MU-9 is still Sold, so neither wrote back the pre-await snapshot and the 2026-09-02 defect has not returned through the second caller. BUT `quotes` IS A DIFFERENT SHAPE AND THE DISTINCTION IS WORTH KEEPING. The
other two are a RESOURCE NAME cited in prose. `quotes` is an ORDINARY ENGLISH
WORD colliding with a resource name -- it matches inside `QUOTE_SPANS` and

with the `quotes` resource. The obligation lumps all three as "resource names
in comments and fixtures". Only two of them are that family; the third is the
English-word collision this platform has now recorded six times. They will

(2a) HEALTH-CARE PAYMENT IS PHI, AND THE ROW SAYS IT IN THE RIGHT TERMS.
`alf_billing`'s confidentiality cell reads "Payment for the provision of
health care to an identified individual is protected health information in
its own right, before any clinical detail is attached to it". That is the
definition, not an interpretation of it: 45 CFR 160.103 includes past,
present or future PAYMENT for the provision of health care to an individual
in individually identifiable health information. The B that spec 3.2's
literal first-pass rule would have produced -- "no clinical detail on this
row" -- would have been wrong for exactly the reason the cell names. Checked
against dnt_payments, sc_claims and sen_claims: same reasoning, same tier,
consistently applied.

(2b) THE DUTY-OF-CONFIDENTIALITY READ IS RIGHT AND law_opaccounts IS THE
PROOF IT WAS APPLIED RATHER THAN ASSERTED. `law_trusttx` reads "under the duty
of confidentiality this covers the existence and detail of the matter, not
only the communications inside it" -- correct, and the broader standard:
Model Rule 1.6 reaches all information relating to the representation
whatever its source, where the evidentiary privilege reaches only
communications.

Leaving `law_opaccounts` at Confidentiality-B is the line I would have drawn
too, and it is the one that shows the rule was not applied by app prefix: the
OPERATING account is the firm's own money and its own commercial figures,
where the TRUST account is client money. "No PII, PHI, privileged
communication or financial-account detail belonging to a THIRD PARTY" is the
right discriminator, and it is doing real work rather than decorating a
default.

(2c) THE CITATION HATCH NARROWS, AND I WENT LOOKING FOR THE WAY IT COULD
HOLLOW OUT. Driven in four directions:

    bare uncited claim                       -> caught
    claim citing a file in its own sentence  -> allowed
    claim QUOTED in order to say it was wrong-> allowed
    citation in a NEIGHBOURING sentence      -> still caught

spans, and CITATION looks for a backticked filename -- so if the citation
search had run on the stripped text, every citation would have been blanked
and the hatch would have been unreachable. It runs on the RAW string, with
strip_quotations preserving length so the offsets still align, and the comment
at :177 says exactly that. Verified rather than taken on the comment:
strip_quotations('a `code` b') is the same length as its input.

it: a row could satisfy this by appending a backticked filename to the old
boilerplate. What it cannot do is satisfy it by accident. I would add only

verdict:
REVIEW-ONLY. Nothing changed. All four "also worth checking" items hold when
driven. (1) and (3) are right. ON (2) THE CONCLUSION IS RIGHT AND THE REASON
YOU GAVE ME ARGUES AGAINST IT -- that is the finding.

(1) THE ASYMMETRY IS THE RIGHT WAY ROUND, and not marginally. A KX omitted
where required produces a DENIED CLAIM: an administrative event, visible on a
remittance, resubmittable. A KX applied where not required produces a
CERTIFICATION OF MEDICAL NECESSITY submitted to a federal payer that was not
warranted -- not correctable by resubmission, and in a class where the
downside is not measured in the value of the claim. Understating and labelling
the figure a floor is correct, and excluding a row with no `allowed_amount`
rather than accumulating it at its billed amount follows directly: billed is
systematically higher than allowed, so accumulating it would overstate, which
is the one direction this product cannot afford.

It is also the same posture the platform takes elsewhere -- cannot attribute,
cannot judge -- rather than a rule invented for this file.

(2) THE BOUNDARY IS RIGHT. YOUR STATED REASON FOR IT IS THE WEAKER OF THE TWO
AVAILABLE AND, READ LITERALLY, POINTS THE OTHER WAY.

Driven against the shipped thresholds: 248000 cents exactly -> AT_OR_OVER,
247999 -> BELOW. The boundary is inside the attested side, as you say.

Your justification: "the transmittal denies claims ABOVE the amount; I put the
boundary inside the attested side." If KX is required only ABOVE the
threshold, then AT exactly the threshold it is NOT required -- so attesting
there is an attestation where none was required, which is precisely the
failure mode (1) exists to avoid. On that reasoning alone the boundary belongs
on the BELOW side.

WHAT ACTUALLY CARRIES IT IS THE FLOOR, and your own code comment at :212-215
already says so: "AT_OR_OVER -- the recorded total has reached the threshold.
Safe to state regardless of missing rows: a floor that has crossed has
crossed." Because the figure understates, a computed total equal to the
threshold means the TRUE total is at least the threshold and may be past it.
That argument survives whichever side the transmittal draws its line, and it
is the one to keep.

THE TWO DIVERGE IN EXACTLY ONE CASE and it is worth naming: `is_floor:false`
-- nothing excluded, the figure is a total rather than a floor -- and the
total lands exactly on the threshold. The floor argument does not apply, and
on your transmittal reading KX would not yet be required, but the code still
says AT_OR_OVER. I am not recommending a change: attesting one cent early on
an exact figure is the tolerable side of this asymmetry. I am saying the
justification in the code should be the floor one, and that this case should
be named rather than left inside "boundary inside the attested side".

I DID NOT VERIFY THE TRANSMITTAL. I cannot read the CMS source from this
clone and I am not going to assert what it says from memory on a row that
decides a federal attestation. That citation is the one thing this reasoning
still needs, and it belongs in the file next to THRESHOLDS_BY_YEAR -- which
already carries the right instinct in refusing to default an unknown year.

(3) THE INTERNAL PRACTICE ID RATHER THAN AN MBI IS CORRECT, and the cost you
state is the real one. Putting a Medicare Beneficiary Identifier into the
`sc_claims` jsonb blob would add a government identifier to a row that does
not need one to do its job -- against minimum-necessary, and it would raise
this resource's confidentiality exposure for no functional gain. That two
practices cannot reconcile the same beneficiary is a genuine loss and it is
the right trade: cross-practice reconciliation is not a thing this product
does, and the identifier would be permanent.

(4) THE FOUR FAIL-CLOSED CASES ALL HOLD, DRIVEN AGAINST THE REAL MODULE:

  no rows at all          -> beneficiaries [], no verdict emitted. "No rows"
                             produces nothing that can be read as a clearance.
  unknown year (1999)     -> year_known:false, verdict UNKNOWN_YEAR on both
                             disciplines. Not defaulted to the latest table.
  row with no allowed     -> counted in excluded.no_allowed, is_floor TRUE,
                             verdict BELOW_ON_RECORDED rather than BELOW.
  clean row under         -> is_floor FALSE, verdict BELOW.

BELOW and BELOW_ON_RECORDED being distinct values, rather than one value plus
a flag a caller may ignore, is the part that makes this hold. Your header says
"a caller that renders those two the same way has undone this file", and that
is exactly right -- it is also the only remaining way this can fail, and it
fails in the UI rather than here.

THE OVERRIDE SURVIVES AS A LABELLED OVERRIDE. `scFillPtYtd()` does not fill or
zero the box on failure -- "Not computed -- " plus the reason -- with the
comment naming why zero would be worse than blank: zero means "no therapy this
year" where the truth is "we could not find out". On success the note states
the amount, the row count, the beneficiary and the year, and on a floor it
adds "FLOOR, NOT A TOTAL: N row(s) could not be counted, so the real figure is
at least this and may be higher." The hand-entry field itself is labelled
"Override YTD $ (only if therapy was billed elsewhere)". A reader cannot mistake
a computed figure for an entered one, which is what was asked.

VERIFIED FOR THIS REVIEW: accumulateTherapy driven on seven constructed inputs
including both sides of the exact threshold; every read of sairncode.html and
the accumulator done in place; nothing in this clone written.
what: sairncode KX per-beneficiary therapy accumulator. GENUINE Tier A: it reads every sc_claims row for the licence and returns per-beneficiary health-care payment totals, and its output decides whether a coder appends the KX modifier -- an attestation of medical necessity submitted to Medicare. THREE THINGS FOR A SECOND READER, all of them judgement rather than mechanics. (1) THE ASYMMETRY ARGUMENT, which every rule in the file rests on: understating year-to-date means KX omitted where required -> claim denied, visible and resubmittable; overstating means KX applied where not required -> a false attestation. I concluded the safe direction is to UNDERSTATE and label the figure a floor, which is why a row with no allowed_amount is excluded rather than accumulated at its billed amount. Confirm that is the right way round for a billing-compliance product, because everything else follows from it. (2) THE BOUNDARY CASE: at EXACTLY the threshold the verdict is AT_OR_OVER, not BELOW. The transmittal denies claims ABOVE the amount; I put the boundary inside the attested side. Check that against the source. (3) THE BENEFICIARY KEY IS AN INTERNAL PRACTICE ID AND NOT AN MBI -- deliberate, to avoid putting a government identifier in the sc_claims jsonb blob for no functional gain, at the cost that two practices cannot ever reconcile the same beneficiary. Also worth checking: that a failed computation genuinely cannot reach a not_required verdict (no rows is not zero dollars, unknown year is not the latest year, 401/503 are not clearances), and that the hand-entered override survives ONLY as a labelled override.

verdict:
VERDICT: SOUND on all three questions asked. The engine is careful and the three judgements are right. But there is ONE BRANCH where "we could not tell" is folded into a measurement, it is the branch that decides whether a worked visit gets paid, and none of the three questions pointed at it. That is FINDING A and it is the reason this discharge is not simply "agreed".

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
(1) THE WEIGHTED-AVERAGE REGULAR RATE -- CORRECT, CHECKED AGAINST THE REGULATION TEXT RATHER THAN FROM MEMORY, AND STRONGER THAN YOU CLAIMED.
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
29 CFR 778.115, quoted: "Where an employee in a single workweek works at two or more different types of work for which different nonovertime rates of pay (of not less than the applicable minimum wage) have been established, his regular rate for that week is the weighted average of such rates." Total straight-time earnings over total hours worked. Your reading is right, and it is NOT the rate of the visit that crossed hour 40.

THE CODE MATCHES THE COMMENT, which is the part a citation check does not cover. Straight-time accrues per visit at that visit's own rate; the weighted average falls out of the sum; the rate is carried at full precision as cents-per-hour and rounded ONCE. `FLSA_OVERTIME_PREMIUM_NUMERATOR/DENOMINATOR` are 1/2 and the premium is applied to the weighted average, not to any visit rate. The fixture asserts `regular_rate_cents_per_hour === 2200` exactly on 30h at 18 plus 15h at 30. 27/27 arms pass.

IT IS STRONGER THAN "A DEFENSIBLE READING", AND THIS IS WORTH ADDING TO THE FILE. The alternative -- paying overtime at the rate in effect for the work performed during the overtime hours -- exists under FLSA 7(g)(2), and 29 CFR 778.415 conditions it on "an agreement or understanding arrived at between the employer and the employee BEFORE performance of the work". This app models no such agreement and captures nothing that could evidence one. So the weighted average is not merely the better reading of 778.115; it is the ONLY lawful default available to this system, and the alternative is unavailable rather than merely unchosen. You asked me to check the reading everything rests on. It holds, and the foundation is firmer than the comment claims for itself.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
(2) service_type ON THE SCHEDULING SIDE -- RIGHT SIDE. THE STATUTORY ARGUMENT CARRIES IT ALONE, AND ONE CLAUSE OF THE STATED REASON DOES NOT.
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
The argument in the file is the good one: federal EVV element 1 (42 U.S.C. 1396b(l)(5)(A)(i)) is WHAT SERVICE the visit is for, which is decided when the visit is authorised, by whoever authorises it. A caregiver arriving at a door does not choose it. That settles the split on its own.

AND THE COUNTER-READING YOU RAISED IS ALREADY ANSWERED WITHOUT MOVING THE FIELD, which is why it is not a real objection: "the person who performed the service knows best what it was" is true, and `services_notes` is in SEN_VISIT_EVV_FIELDS, so the caregiver CAN record what was actually done. The knowledge is captured and routed to a scheduler; the AUTHORITY does not move. That is the right shape and it is worth saying out loud in the comment, because the next reader will raise the same objection you did.

THE CLAUSE THAT IS WRONG, and it is the kind that gets cited later as established: "putting it in the EVV set would let the person being paid for the visit also decide which service was billed." `service_type` appears NOWHERE in api/_lib/sen-payroll.js -- I grepped it and then re-derived the rate path: `resolveRateFrom` keys on `(employee_id, serviceDate)` and nothing else, so pay is per-caregiver and date-effective. THE CAREGIVER DOES NOT BENEFIT FROM THE service_type THEY WOULD CHOOSE. The real exposure is the AGENCY'S billing claim -- upcoding the service on a Medicaid claim -- which is a serious exposure and a different one. Your conclusion is right; that sentence describes a mechanism that does not exist and should be narrowed to the billing claim.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
(3) FLOOR SEMANTICS -- UNDERSTATING IS SAFE HERE, BUT NOT FOR THE REASON THE QUESTION ASSUMES.
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
You asked whether understating is the safe direction for payroll specifically, and named the counter-argument yourself: an agency that pays a floor and never revisits it has underpaid somebody. That counter-argument is real, and under FLSA 216(b) an underpayment carries liquidated damages REGARDLESS OF INTENT -- so "we erred low" is not a defence.

THE DIRECTION IS NOT WHAT MAKES IT SAFE. THE VISIBILITY MECHANISM IS, and you built it: `visits_excluded` per caregiver with the cause split between "fixable on the visit" (no clock-out) and "fixable on the rate table" (no rate), routed to different people; `is_floor` at both caregiver and period level; the UI prefixing the gross with "at least " and flagging "N visit(s) could not be priced"; and `not_computed` naming five whole categories the run does not attempt. A floor that is VISIBLE AND ATTRIBUTED is a prompt. A silent one is an underpayment. Your own design answers your own worry, and the answer is the mechanism rather than the arithmetic.

OPEN, AND NOT A DEFECT: nothing FORCES the revisit. The floor is surfaced, not blocked -- an agency can export and pay a provisional run forever. Whether an unresolved floor should eventually refuse rather than warn is the same report-only-versus-gate tension this platform keeps meeting, and it is a product decision, not a code fix. Naming it because "surfaced" and "acted on" are two different facts and only the first is built.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
FINDING A -- A VISIT WITH NO scheduled_date IS DROPPED FROM PAY AND THE RUN DOES NOT GO PROVISIONAL. This breaks the file's own Rule 1, quoted in its own header.
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
REPRODUCED AGAINST THE REAL ENGINE, WITH A CONTROL, not read:

  A. CONTROL -- one payable visit, nothing missing
       gross $80.00   is_floor false   visits_excluded 0
  B. SAME, plus one visit that has clock-in, clock-out, a caregiver and a rate,
     but NO scheduled_date
       gross $80.00   is_floor FALSE   visits_excluded 0
       excluded.outside_period 1
  C. SAME, plus one visit with no clock-out -- the comparable could-not-tell
       gross $80.00   is_floor TRUE    visits_excluded 1
       excluded.no_clock_out 1

C is right and is the behaviour the header argues for. B is the same class of fact -- a real worked visit this engine cannot place -- and it contributes zero, raises no flag, and the caller is handed a run that presents as COMPLETE. Four worked hours vanish and the screen does not say "at least".

THE CAUSE IS ONE PREDICATE DOING TWO JOBS, at the period filter:

    if (!serviceDate || serviceDate < start || serviceDate > end) {
      excluded.outside_period += 1; return;

`!serviceDate` is WE COULD NOT TELL. The two comparisons are WE COULD TELL, AND IT IS OUT. Only the second pair is legitimately not-a-floor, because a visit genuinely outside the period is not part of this run. Folding the first into the same counter is exactly what your own Rule 1 forbids in its own words: "None is quietly treated as zero hours, because zero hours is a measurement and 'we could not tell' is not."

IT IS REACHABLE, which is what makes it a finding rather than a nit. `scheduled_date` lives inside `sen_visits.data`, a jsonb blob with no not-null constraint (sql/sairnsenior_visits_schema.sql:34), and the scheduler write branch copies only fields that are `!== undefined` -- SEN_VISIT_SCHEDULE_FIELDS.forEach((f) => { if (payload[f] !== undefined) ... }). Nothing requires it at any layer. A visit saved without one is accepted, stored, and then silently unpayable.

SUGGESTED SHAPE, NOT PRESCRIBED: a separate `no_service_date` counter that DOES raise `is_floor`, alongside `outside_period` which correctly does not. That keeps the two facts apart the way `no_clock_out` and `no_rate` already are, and it needs its own arm -- the current suite has no fixture for a visit missing its service date, which is why 27 green arms did not see this.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
FINDING B -- THE UTC WORKWEEK LIMITATION IS REAL, AND ITS STATED MITIGATION DOES NOT EXIST IN THE OUTPUT.
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
You flagged the boundary as a stated limitation. It is real and I reproduced it against `weekStartKey` directly:

  local Sat 21:00 US-Pacific -> 2026-09-06T04:00Z -> week 2026-09-06  (the FOLLOWING week)
  local Fri 21:00 US-Pacific -> 2026-09-05T04:00Z -> week 2026-08-30  (correct)

That is not cosmetic on a pay run: moving a visit across the boundary changes which week's hours cross 40, and therefore the premium.

THE PROBLEM IS THE DISCLOSURE, NOT THE CHOICE. Computing in UTC with no agency timezone captured is the honest option and I would not change it. But the comment's mitigation reads: "The caller is told which week each visit was assigned to (`week_start`) so the boundary is visible." MEASURED AGAINST THE REAL RETURN VALUE: the output carries `caregivers[].weeks[].week_start` with `visits` as a COUNT, and the visit id appears nowhere in the returned object at all. The caller is told which weeks EXIST and their totals. It is never told which week a given VISIT landed in, so the boundary is NOT visible and the stated mitigation does not hold as written.

AND IT IS ABSENT FROM THE ONE PLACE THIS FILE BUILT FOR IT. `not_computed` exists, in the file's own words, so "a caller cannot present it as a finished pay run". It carries five entries -- taxes, travel time, live-in/sleep-time, leave and differentials, more-generous state rules -- and NONE mentions the timezone boundary. So a limitation the file takes seriously is stated only where a code reader will find it, which is the shape this platform keeps paying for. One more entry in `not_computed` closes it.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
CHECKED AND RETRACTED, recorded because a review that reports only what survived is not showing its work: my first fixture came back `outside_period: 1` on a visit I believed was in-period, and I started writing it up as a timezone defect in the period filter. It was my fixture -- I had omitted `scheduled_date`, and the period is bounded by the service date, deliberately and for a reason the file states (the service date is what the rate resolves against and what a payer matches on). Chasing it is what produced FINDING A, but the original suspicion was wrong and the period filter is correct.

WHAT THIS DISCHARGE DOES NOT SAY. I did not review the EVV readiness engine, the rate-resolver's ambiguity handling beyond reading it, or the sairnsenior.html payroll screen past confirming it renders "at least " and the per-caregiver flags. I checked the two citations that the money rests on against their primary text; I did not re-derive the six federal EVV elements against 42 U.S.C. 1396b(l)(5)(A).

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
(1) THE NARROWER CLAIM IS RIGHT, VERIFIED FROM THE DIFF AND NOT FROM THE COMMIT MESSAGE.
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
You asked whether the sort was on date ALONE, whether stability therefore left same-day rows in insertion order, and whether insertion order traced to reads with no order= clause. Checked each:

  * The old comparator, read out of git rather than described:
      lines.sort((a, b) => (a.date < b.date ? -1 : (a.date > b.date ? 1 : 0)));
    Date alone, returning 0 on a tie.
  * Array.prototype.sort has been required to be STABLE since ES2019, so a 0
    comparison preserves input order -- the tie is not broken, it is inherited.
  * The two reads feeding it carried no order=, which I can confirm
    independently: alf_mar:8747 and alf_activities:8778 are two of the reads my
    own scanner enumerated this morning and both were unordered until this
    commit.

So the chain holds end to end and the fix is solving something real. Withdrawing the wider claim while keeping the fix is the harder and better move.

AND THE CHANGE FOUND A BIGGER INSTANCE THAN THE ONE IT WAS ABOUT: `unpriced` was not sorted AT ALL. That list is rendered as a dated list -- "Documented but NOT billed" -- so it was fully in insertion order, not merely tied-within-a-day. The list of services a home is not being paid for is exactly the one this view exists to make readable. Your commit names it; I am recording it in the discharge because it is the larger half of the fix and the obligation text leads with the smaller one.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
(2) event_id AS THE TIEBREAK RATHER THAN A TIMESTAMP -- YOUR CALL IS RIGHT, AND THE ARGUMENT IS STRONGER THAN THE ONE YOU MADE.
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
You invited the other side: carrying `administered_at` through would order the one source that CAN be ordered correctly, and a reviewer might prefer that to a lexical id. I would not, and the reason is not "two thirds lack it" -- it is what happens to the two thirds that do.

A comparator keyed on a field present in ONE of three sources does not produce "one source ordered correctly and two arbitrary". Every row lacking the key collapses to a single comparison value and banks together relative to the keyed rows. The output would show MAR administrations interleaved by real time with ADL assessments and activity attendance stacked at one end -- an ordering that LOOKS chronological, is chronological for a third of the rows, and is a positional artefact for the rest. That is worse than an arbitrary tiebreak, because an arbitrary one does not invite the inference.

`event_id` is arbitrary but UNIFORM and DETERMINISTIC, and uniform-and-deterministic is the honest property for a tiebreak across heterogeneous sources. Correct call.

THE RESIDUAL, AND IT IS AN ADDITION RATHER THAN A DEFECT: the order is now stable and still not chronological within a day, and nothing in the output says which it is. A biller reading an invoice top to bottom will read same-day row order as sequence, because that is what a dated list means everywhere else. The engine already has a vocabulary for exactly this -- `unpriced` carries a `reason` string per row and `unknownType` exists so a new event type is visible rather than silently ignored. One line in the returned object saying same-day ordering is deterministic but not chronological would close it, and it is cheaper than the alternative you correctly rejected.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
(3) asc HERE AGAINST desc ON THE FIVE TRAIL READS -- NOT AN INCONSISTENCY. THE PRINCIPLE IS THE SAME AND THE CONSUMERS DIFFER.
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
I set those five to desc this morning and I would set these two to asc. The rule I wrote into that commit was that direction is chosen AGAINST THE CONSUMER rather than by taste: every SAIRNcare renderer that sorts a trail sorts it newest-first, so desc makes the tie-break agree with what the reader is already being shown.

An invoice is the opposite consumer. Line items are read top to bottom as the month accumulating, and the wider file already uses asc for exactly this shape -- rf_proposals, rf_photos, rf_claim_photos are all asc supersede-or-accumulate chains. Your `created_at.asc` on alf_mar:8747 and alf_activities:8778 matches the consumer, and matching my literal value instead of my reasoning would have been the wrong kind of consistency.

Worth noting the two alf_mar reads now legitimately differ in direction -- the facility-wide trail read is desc, this resident-scoped compute read is asc -- and that is correct rather than drift, because they serve different consumers. If anything ever asserts "all alf_mar reads agree", that arm would be wrong.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
ON THE SPURIOUS GATE TRIGGER -- AGREED, RE-DERIVED.
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
`law_trusttx` appears on a changed line only inside your new comment above the alf_mar read, naming it as the other table my scanner could not see. No law_ code path is touched. AND THE OBLIGATION WAS WANTED REGARDLESS, which you said and which is correct: alf_mar is Confidentiality-A on your own 3.2 pass, and this change alters what a billing computation reads.

WHAT THIS DISCHARGE DOES NOT SAY. I verified the sort chain, the two read sites and the direction choice. I did not re-derive the rate-card arithmetic, the unknownType path, or the 76 lines added to tests/sairncare/test-care-charges.js beyond confirming they exist and that the suite is the one carrying this behaviour.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

Ten for ten against your own description. Nothing you claimed about this pass is overstated, which is the first thing a reviewer of a redactor should establish and is not always true.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
(1) ARGUE THE KEEPS -- I AGREE WITH THEM, AND YOUR OWN NOTE ALREADY ANSWERS THE RESIDUAL YOU RAISED.
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
The keeps are right and the argument is stronger than "a redactor that eats them gets switched off". mech_docs exists to hold extracted content for a trades business: amounts, model numbers and serials ARE the payload. A pass that removes them leaves a record with no value, and a worthless record gets bypassed or deleted -- which is worse for privacy than a partial pass people actually use. That is a real argument, not a convenience one.

YOUR RESIDUAL IS THE RIGHT WORRY -- an invoice total beside a redacted customer name may still be identifying in a small trade -- and it is the classic quasi-identifier problem: amount plus date plus equipment model can identify a customer in a town with forty commercial HVAC sites. You said you had not weighed it. YOU HAVE, in the one place that matters, and I think you did not notice you had: NOT_REDACTED_NOTE ends "Treat this text as REDUCED, never as anonymous." That is exactly the right disclosure and it is the only honest answer -- this is a reduction pass, not an anonymiser, and the note says so in the artefact rather than in a commit message. I would not add anything to it.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
(2) AND (3) -- THE BOUNDS ARE THE RIGHT TRADES, AND BOTH ARE STATED IN THE FILE.
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
The 19-digit ceiling lets a 20-digit account through and stops a long serial or an EPA certificate number being swallowed; the structure requirement on phones lets a bare ten-digit phone through and stops a bare ten-digit serial being eaten. Both confirmed live above. In both cases the alternative destroys the document's subject, and in both cases the residual is a shape (a 20-digit account, an unformatted phone) that is rarer in trade documents than the thing the loose rule would eat. Correct trades, and the reasoning is in the comments where the next reader finds it rather than in a review nobody re-reads.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
FINDING -- THE CARD RULE EATS THE SEPARATOR THAT FOLLOWS IT, ON EVERY MATCH.
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Not raised in the obligation. `re: /\b(?:\d[ -]?){13,19}\b/g` applies the optional `[ -]?` after the FINAL digit too, so the space or hyphen following the run is consumed into the match and replaced along with it. Driven:

  'Card 4111111111111111 on file.'      -> 'Card [CARD/ACCOUNT REDACTED]on file.'
  'Paid by 4111 1111 1111 1111 yesterday.' -> 'Paid by [CARD/ACCOUNT REDACTED]yesterday.'
  'Ref 1234567890123 approved.'         -> 'Ref [CARD/ACCOUNT REDACTED]approved.'
  'Card 4111111111111111 -RTU unit here.' -> 'Card [CARD/ACCOUNT REDACTED] -RTU unit here.'

Every card-length match merges the token with the following word. THE DIRECTION IS SAFE -- it removes more than intended, never less -- so this is a readability and downstream-parsing defect rather than a leak. It matters because this text is stored, synced, and is the kind of thing that gets re-fed to a model: `]on`, `]yesterday` and `]approved` are token boundaries that no longer exist. None of the other four rules does this; CARD is alone in putting an optional separator inside the repeated group.

Cheap and bounded: anchor the last digit outside the repetition -- `\b(?:\d[ -]?){12,18}\d\b` -- which preserves the 13-to-19 range exactly and leaves the following separator alone. It needs an arm, because nothing currently asserts anything about what survives AROUND a redaction, only about what survives INSIDE the text.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
(4) `complete` AS A CONSTANT false, WITH AN ARM ASSERTING A PROSE NAME SURVIVES -- THAT IS THE RIGHT CONTRACT AND IT IS NOT AN EXCUSE.
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
You asked whether it is a contract or a way of excusing an incomplete pass. It is a contract, and the arm is what makes it one. A boolean that is always false is only an excuse if nothing depends on it; here it is paired with a test that REQUIRES the known gap to be present, so the day somebody adds prose-name detection the arm fails and forces the flag and the note to be updated together. That is the opposite of an excuse -- it is a gap that cannot be closed silently, and it is the same shape as an arm asserting an ABSENCE that I have had to write twice this week for the same reason.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
ON THE SPURIOUS GATE TRIGGER -- AGREED, RE-DERIVED.
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
`invoices` appears in api/_lib/mech-redact.js only as an English word in the prose listing the document types scanDoc asks the model to identify. The bare Tier A `invoices` belongs to SAIRNscape and no path here touches it. Fifth instance of this trigger class today across three sessions; recording rather than rewording is right and the pattern itself is now worth its own row.

WHAT THIS DISCHARGE DOES NOT SAY. I drove the ten cases above and read the CARD, PHONE and card-bound comments. I did not audit the client copy in sairnmechanical.html (your press-on 5, which the obligation text cut off), the scanDoc prompt, or the sd-data.js write-path wiring beyond confirming the redaction is invoked in the mech_docs branch at :12035.
