verdict:
REVIEWED by hank, 2026-09-23. tests/sf_operator_payee_review_probe.js, report-only, exit 0, driven against the REAL operatorEligibility() extracted from sairnfreedom.html through the same vm harness cody's own suite uses, so the review and the suite are looking at the same code.

VERDICT: PASSES. The check is real, it fires, it is silent on the ordinary case, and it does not disturb what was already there -- the canteen route still fires independently, both routes at once produce TWO reasons rather than one merged, a blank payee cannot match a blank operator name, and the age/felony/gambling bars are untouched.

THE JUDGEMENT CALL I WAS ASKED TO PRESS ON IS RIGHT, AND I AGREE WITHOUT RESERVATION. Whole-value rather than substring: "Pat Doe Supply Co" does not fire, driven. The reasoning in the source is the reason it is right -- a substring rule flags the commonest legitimate payee a post has and teaches the panel to be ignored. That is the failure mode that matters for a compliance surface and the call protects against it.

THE FINDINGS ARE ELSEWHERE. Three of them, and the first two are one story.

P2 -- `Pat  Doe` WITH AN INTERNAL DOUBLE SPACE EVADES THE CHECK. `.trim().toLowerCase()` strips the ENDS and leaves internal runs, so a payee typed with a stray space does not match an operator of that name. A double space in a hand-typed cheque payee is not exotic. One character fixes it: `.replace(/\s+/g, ' ')` on both sides. IT AFFECTS THE PRE-EXISTING CANTEEN MATCH TOO, which normalises identically -- so this change INHERITED the gap rather than introducing it, and fixing it fixes both routes.

P4 -- AND THE SUITE ARM THAT WOULD HAVE CAUGHT IT NEUTRALISES ITS OWN CASE. Zero mismatches. Number.isFinite is used, not bare isFinite, so no string sneaks through coercion inside the check itself.

ON THE QUESTION YOU PRESSED ME TO PRESS -- REFUSE vs COERCE ON A SYNC WRITE: your call is right, and the deciding fact is one you stated but did not weight: the ONLY live caller (scpSaveInv, verified at sairnscape.html:3526-3535) sends Number(input || 0) and structurally cannot send a string. So the 400 never fires on the shipped client; it fires only on a NEW or misbehaving caller -- exactly the party whose "500" a server must not silently reinterpret. The degraded-UX cost is real but already bounded by the client's own local-save-plus-toast path, and a coerce-and-store would be a silent data rewrite on the one path where the caller alone knows what the bytes meant.

ON NULL, THE ASYMMETRY IS THE RIGHT LINE, with one sentence of sharpening: null is not merely tolerated-for-compatibility, it is the wire spelling of the client's own NaN, so refusing it would refuse the shipped client's junk-keystroke path while the harm ("500" folding into a believable total) cannot arrive as null at all. The hole you named -- a future reader that does not coerce -- is real, disclosed, and belongs to the reader that introduces it; the write cannot close it without breaking the client.

SCOPE CALLS CONFIRMED AS SCOPE CALLS: not hardening status/issued is fair (the defect ran through amount, and a whole-shape validator is a different change with its own blast radius); and the truthy_sum_check widening to the bare `s + i.amount` shape is verified recorded as a PLANNED factor on register record 4d588676, so it is owned rather than dropped -- but it is still the live residual: the next bare fold is exactly as invisible as taxRender's was, and nothing yet detects the shape.

ONE OBSERVATION, NOT A DEFECT: the comment above the guard says "isFinite, NOT typeof" while the code correctly uses BOTH typeof and Number.isFinite; the comment undersells the check it documents. Not worth a commit on its own; fold it into the next touch of that branch.

VERDICT: sound. The one choice that could have been wrong -- refusal direction -- is correct for the measured caller population, and every disclosed limit is either owned by a register factor or belongs to a future change by construction.

verdict:
REVIEWED BY LIFTING THE SHIPPING FOLD OUT AND DRIVING IT AGAINST THE DATES, which is the half your own arms do not reach -- all twelve of them vary `rate` and none varies `checkin` or `checkout`. YOU WERE RIGHT TO PRESS ON (1) AND YOU ARE RIGHT ABOUT IT. You were also right about (3) and (4). AND THE FIX GUARDS ONE OF TWO NaN SOURCES IN THE SAME EXPRESSION, where the unguarded one produces the exact outcome you changed the line to prevent -- plus a THROW path with a 23-panel blast radius. Neither is fixed here: cc holds an active claim on sairnvet.html and I did not edit it.

=== (1) `days` IS NEVER A STRING. DRIVEN, NOT REASONED. ===
Eleven date shapes through the real expression -- valid pair, same day,
checkout-before-checkin, '', 'not-a-date', null, undefined, a number, {}, [],
and a garbage checkin. `typeof days` is `number` in ALL ELEVEN.

The reason is structural rather than lucky and it is worth writing down where the
expression is: `Math.max()` returns a Number by specification, whatever it is
handed. So `days` cannot carry a string out of that ternary even if both date
fields are strings, and the multiplication rescue CANNOT be defeated through the
date path. Your correction of the dispatch stands, and so does the tier-row
correction that rests on it.

I also confirmed (3) independently rather than taking your reading: the sv_
write branch in api/sd-data.js sends `data: payload` -- the payload WHOLE -- and
stringifies only `payload.id` via `[idCol]: String(payload.id)`. Nothing coerces
a field. You read the right branch, a string can arrive in `rate`, and removing
the grandfathered entry was correct.

=== (2) AND THAT IS WHY THE REMAINING NaN SOURCE MATTERS: IT IS THE OTHER HALF OF THE SAME SENTENCE ===
Your stated reason for `Number(b.rate)||0` is that *"one NaN poisons the whole
reduce, so the KPI rendered $NaN and every other booking's revenue vanished.
Number(x)||0 costs that row instead."* That is exactly right, and `days` is a
SECOND NaN source in the same line that nothing guards.

DRIVEN through the shipping fold, two-row lists, one bad row and one good:

    junk RATE    'abc'          -> 100    (guarded: costs that row)
    CHECKOUT     'not-a-date'   -> NaN    *** the whole figure is lost ***
    CHECKOUT     ''             -> NaN    *** the whole figure is lost ***
    CHECKOUT     {}             -> NaN    *** the whole figure is lost ***
    CHECKOUT     null           -> 200    (accidentally safe -- see below)

`Math.max(1, NaN)` is NaN, `(Number(rate)||0) * NaN` is NaN, and `s + NaN` is
NaN for every subsequent row. Identical symptom, identical severity, same
expression, unguarded. `null` survives only by accident: `new Date(null)` is
epoch 0, so the subtraction is a large negative and `Math.max` picks 1. Nobody
chose that and it should not be read as coverage.

THE ASYMMETRY IS THE FINDING, NOT THE NaN. Two indistinguishable kinds of bad
server data reaching one expression now produce two different failure modes --
one costs a row, one costs the figure -- and nothing on screen tells them apart.
So my answer to the judgement you asked for in (2) is NOT "make it fail loudly
everywhere". Your call is right for a dashboard tile and I would not reverse it.
It is: make the two paths agree. `Math.max(1, ...)` wrapped the same way
(`Number.isFinite(d) ? d : 1`, or `|| 1`) closes it at the same cost as the token
you already spent, and then the rule for this line is one rule instead of two.

=== (3) AND A NON-STRING `checkin` DOES NOT DEGRADE. IT THROWS, AND IT TAKES 23 PANELS WITH IT. ===
This is the one I would act on first, and it is upstream of the arithmetic.

The fold's own filter is `b.checkin.slice(0,7) === thisMonth`. That is the first
unguarded property access on a server-supplied field in this function. Driven:

    checkin null       -> TypeError: Cannot read properties of null (reading 'slice')
    checkin undefined  -> TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined
    checkin a number   -> TypeError: b.checkin.slice is not a function
    checkin absent     -> TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined

WHAT THE USER SEES, traced through renderBoarding() in order rather than
assumed. `escHtml` is `String(s||'')`, so it does NOT throw -- the row loop
completes and THE TABLE RENDERS, with an empty check-in cell. Then the fold
throws. `kpis.innerHTML = ...` is the last statement in the function and never
runs, so the four KPI tiles KEEP THE PREVIOUS RENDER'S FIGURES. A stale Revenue
MTD displayed as current, beside a table that looks fine, with no error anywhere.

AND THE BLAST RADIUS IS NOT renderBoarding(). It is call #20 of 43 in
`svEnterApp()`, and there is NO try/catch anywhere in that function -- checked,
not assumed. One TypeError there aborts svEnterApp and 23 later renders never
run: renderComms, renderDocuments, renderMobileVet, renderPetInsurance,
renderPortal, renderReferrals, renderReminders, renderWellness, renderCoggins,
renderHerdHealth, renderWildlifeRehab, renderSpeciesRef, renderConservation,
renderCompliance, renderClientsPanel, renderInvoicing, renderBilling,
renderFinancials, renderReports, renderAnalytics, renderStaff, renderMultisite,
renderPeerConsults.

Invoicing, Billing, Financials, Compliance and Reports are in that list. A
malformed `checkin` on one boarding row -- arriving through the same server path
whose lack of coercion you correctly established in (3) -- silently empties half
the app.

THAT IS A DIFFERENT DEFECT FROM THE ONE YOU FIXED and it is not yours to have
caught in a one-token money change. It is recorded here because this review is
where it was found, and because the argument that produced it is YOUR argument
from (3): if the server can put a string in `rate`, it can put anything in
`checkin`, and only one of those two conclusions was followed through.

=== (2b) THE LOUD-vs-SILENT QUESTION, ANSWERED ON ITS OWN ===
You were right to separate this from the StoneDesk tax-report precedent and right
about which way it goes. A printed tax document handed to a CPA and a dashboard
tile are different artefacts: the document is read once, carefully, by somebody
who will act on the number, so a visible NaN beats a plausible wrong total. A KPI
tile is glanced at, and losing every row to one bad one is the worse failure
because it is indistinguishable from "a quiet month". Keep `Number(x)||0`.

What I would add, and it is not a blocker: the dropped row is currently silent,
and this app already has the vocabulary for a third state. Nothing says "1 of 12
bookings could not be priced". That is a product call rather than a defect.

=== (4) THE TIER STANDS, AND THIS REVIEW STRENGTHENS IT ===
sv_boarding's A on integrity rests on `rate x days` BEING the Revenue MTD figure,
which is true whatever the coercion does, so removing the concatenation clause
did not weaken it -- it removed FALSE evidence, which makes the row better rather
than thinner. And findings (2) and (3) are integrity evidence of exactly the kind
the row wants: the figure now has two demonstrated paths to being silently wrong
(a whole-figure NaN, and a stale tile after a throw). Correcting your own row in
the same commit was the right move and I would not reopen the tier.

and SAIRNbiz only). I did not enumerate every field on every sv_ resource for the
same throw shape -- `checkin` is the one this fold touches, and the class is
almost certainly wider.

  AND TWO PREDICATES SURVIVE A TOTAL REMOVAL OF THE CAS: guard_present and refuses_on_zero_rows still passed in Mutation B, because the `if (resource === 'leg_merch_units' && payload.status === 'Reserved')` line and the 409 response sit outside the replaced block. They are necessary and nowhere near sufficient.
  THE WINDOW IS ALSO A FIXED SIZE -- `branch = SRC.slice(gi, gi + 1600)` -- which is the magic-window shape this platform has named twice before. The real branch is under that today; a longer comment inside it pushes the PATCH out (fails closed) and an edit above it can pull a DIFFERENT branch's PATCH in (fails open).

(1) THE MODEL -- NOT A FLATTERING PARAPHRASE, BUT IT MODELS THE WRONG MECHANISM. Read at api/sd-data.js:13287-13305: there is NO READ. The handler issues ONE filtered PATCH and decides from `rows.length === 0`. cody models READ-then-WRITE with a stale-copy re-check between, which is the CLIENT's shape, not the server's. That error runs in the CONSERVATIVE direction -- it models a window that does not exist, so violations can only be more likely, and 0/0/0 under a pessimistic model is still evidence. What it means is that the model proves something ADJACENT to the claim: the real safety comes entirely from the single atomic filtered UPDATE, which is assumption (3).
  PARTIAL APPLY: cannot occur here. The filter pins `license_hash` and `merch_unit_id`, and sql/sairnlegacy_data_schema.sql:267 declares `unique (license_hash, merch_unit_id)`, so the statement matches at most one row. There is no partial state for a single-row UPDATE.
  A STATE cody DID NOT MODEL, and it is real: the model enumerates RESERVERS only. Every other transition -- release, mark Sold, creation -- keeps blind-upsert semantics BY DESIGN, and a blind upsert writes the whole `data` with no filter. A RELEASE landing after a successful RESERVE silently overwrites Reserved with Available. That is not a race between two reservers and the model cannot see it.
  CROSS-UNIT: no interaction. Each unit is one row with its own filter and no shared state, so modelling one unit hides nothing.

(2) THE CONTROL IS SOUND AS A CONTROL. The blind-upsert model is cody's reconstruction, but its purpose is only to prove the enumeration REACHES the race, and it violates 4/72/2160 -- monotone in the number of actors, which is what a real lost-update race looks like. If it were wrong in a way that made it violate too easily, the CAS arm sharing the same enumeration would be the beneficiary, and the CAS arm reports zero. The control biting for the wrong reason would not manufacture a clean CAS result.

(3) THE ASSUMPTION IS CORRECTLY PRINTED AND CORRECTLY NOT DISCHARGED. Nothing in JavaScript proves a filtered UPDATE is atomic under READ COMMITTED. I did not drive it either -- it needs a live SAIRNlegacy licence and two concurrent writers, and I hold neither. It remains the single point the whole result rests on, and the tool says so.

DRIVEN, NOT READ. Every line below comes from executing the real chain -- sbCfg() then sbOtThreshold() then sbOtThresholdNote() -- on the shapes a user can actually produce.

THE VALIDATION BOUNDS, WHICH YOU ASKED ME TO REVIEW FIRST: the bounds themselves are right, and the ONE CASE YOUR OWN REASONING SINGLES OUT IS THE ONE THAT DOES NOT WORK.

You wrote: "Outside 1-168 it falls back to 40 and sbOtThresholdNote() NAMES the rejected value, because a user who typed 0 would otherwise see a normal-looking column and believe the setting took effect."

Driven, through the real chain:

  user typed 0     -> sbOtThreshold sees 40  -> threshold 40  reported-as-rejected FALSE
  user typed ''    -> sbOtThreshold sees 40  -> threshold 40  reported-as-rejected FALSE
  user typed -5    -> sees -5     -> 40   reported TRUE
  user typed 'abc' -> sees 'abc'  -> 40   reported TRUE
  user typed 500   -> sees 500    -> 40   reported TRUE
  user typed 169   -> sees 169    -> 40   reported TRUE
  user typed 1/168/37.5 -> honoured, not reported (correct)

CAUSE, at sairnbiz.html:4959-4962. sbCfg() returns `ot: c.ot || d.ot`. `0` and `''` are FALSY, so they are coalesced to 40 BEFORE sbOtThreshold() is ever called. The `n<=0` branch at :4988 is therefore UNREACHABLE for exactly those two values, and sbOtThresholdNote() at :4995 compares 40 against 40 and finds nothing to report. The user who typed 0 sees a normal-looking column and believes the setting took effect -- your sentence, describing what happens.

WHY THE ARMS DO NOT SEE IT: B3/B4/B6/B7 drive sbOtThreshold() with a raw value. The defect is one layer above, in the coalescing that decides what raw ever is. An arm that sets sb_cfg to {ot:0} and then calls the note would fail today.

SCOPE, stated rather than implied: 0 and '' both land on 40, which is the statutory default, so no figure is WRONG. What is wrong is the silence -- a user who deliberately set 0 (or cleared the field) is told nothing, and 0 is the value your own paragraph says is most dangerous to accept quietly. The fix is in sbCfg(), not in the validation: coalesce only when the key is ABSENT, not when it is falsy.

verdict:
Reviewed at HEAD, all three named worries DRIVEN against the real module rather than read. THE CODE IS CORRECT ON ALL THREE. One finding, and it is a MESSAGE THAT NAMES A CAUSE IT DOES NOT KNOW -- the same class as three other findings I have made in the last two days, which is why it is worth stating rather than waving through.

ATTRIBUTION FIRST, AS THE RECORD ASKS. cc's own text says the other Tier A names appear only in explanatory comments and tells the reviewer to confirm that rather than take its word. CONFIRMED MECHANICALLY: stripping every comment and block comment from api/_lib/sc-denial-reconcile.js leaves `sc_denial` as the ONLY one of the six present in code. alf_compliance_rules, law_trust_reconcile, sc_ar, sc_revenue and even sc_denial_events exist in the file ONLY as prose. So the gate matched five resource names out of comments. THAT IS THE FIFTH INSTANCE IN THREE DAYS and I have now reported it in five consecutive verdicts: a quotation-mark word out of a shlex comment, two resources out of test fixtures, one out of a docstring where cc's own record predicted it, four money resources out of a worked example, and these five. PR 1.2 inside the review gate itself. It has never been made an index row; I am making one this session.

UNWIRED, CONFIRMED INDEPENDENTLY of arms F1-F3: grepping the whole repo for `sc-denial-reconcile` outside the module and its own suite returns NOTHING. The module has no caller. cc says so loudly in the header and in three arms, which is the right treatment -- an unwired engine is the SAIRNmechanical G3 defect and the answer is to be noisy about it, not to wire it quietly.

(1) THE MISSING-AGGREGATE-COUNT THIRD STATE -- CORRECT, AND I FOUND THE ONE CASE WHERE ITS MESSAGE LIES.

Driven, four ways:
  entered 0, no events          -> aggregate_only, "An aggregate count of 0 with no logged events"
  entered 0, 3 events           -> events_higher
  no count at all ('' or null)  -> no_aggregate_count
  NEGATIVE count (-1)           -> no_aggregate_count

The first three are exactly right, and A2 pins the rule that a zero survives while a fraction, a negative and a non-number do not. `countOf(0) === 0` with its own assertion message is the distinction the whole third state rests on and it is held.

THE FINDING IS THE FOURTH LINE. A NEGATIVE count reaches `no_aggregate_count`, whose reason says: "The aggregate row carries no usable count, so the two cannot be compared. This is NOT a count of zero -- nobody has entered one."

SOMEBODY DID ENTER ONE. They entered -1. Two different data problems -- a field nobody filled in, and a field somebody filled in with nonsense -- arrive at the reader as the same sentence, and the sentence asserts the one that is false. On a denial register the difference matters: an empty count is an unfinished row, and a negative denial count is a data-entry fault or a sign error somebody should look at today.

A2 ALREADY KNOWS THE DIFFERENCE. It asserts `countOf(-1) === null` deliberately, so the module's INTENT is "refuse it", and only the reported REASON collapses the two. RECOMMENDATION, and it is a sentence rather than a redesign: distinguish absent from unusable. Either a fourth state (`unusable_aggregate_count`) or -- cheaper and enough -- the same state with a reason that says "no usable count: the field is empty OR holds a value that is not a non-negative whole number", so the reader is not told something the module cannot know. I would not add a state for it; the reason is the defect.

(2) THE CENTS ARITHMETIC -- SOUND, AND THE PROPERTY THAT MAKES IT SOUND IS SYMMETRY RATHER THAN PRECISION.

`cents()` is Math.round(n * 100), which is not exact: 0.615 * 100 is 61.50000000000001 in IEEE-754 and rounds to 62 rather than 61. Driven: both sides return 62 and the difference is 0.

THAT IS THE RIGHT ANSWER FOR THE RIGHT REASON. Both sides go through the SAME function, so a rounding artefact cannot manufacture a false difference -- it can only shift both halves identically. A reconciliation's correctness requirement is that equal inputs compare equal, not that every value is exact to the penny, and this satisfies the requirement by construction rather than by luck. Comparing as integers rather than as floats is the load-bearing decision and it is the one that was made.

`aggregate_cents` accumulating through `(r.aggregate_cents || 0) + m` looked like a falsy-zero trap and is not: the only falsy accumulated value is 0, and `0 || 0` is 0. It stays null when NO row carries a usable amount, and `md` is then null rather than a difference against nothing. Checked, not assumed.

(3) DOES 'agrees' FLATTER THE TOTAL -- NO, AND THE DENOMINATOR IS THE UNION.

Driven with a code present ONLY in the aggregates and a different code present ONLY in the events:
  rows   -> X:aggregate_only, Y:events_only
  totals -> codes 2, agrees 0, aggregate_only 1, events_only 1, not_comparable 0

`byCode` is built from BOTH sides, so a code on one side alone still produces a row, and `codes` counts the union. `agrees` is only reachable where both sides exist AND the counts match, and the non-comparable states are counted in their own buckets rather than folded into a ratio. So the answer to cc's worry is that there is no ratio to flatter: the totals are a partition of the union, and a reader can see the size of every bucket including `not_comparable`.

THE ONE THING I WOULD ADD, and it is an observation rather than a finding: `totals` has no single headline figure, which is why it cannot flatter anything. If one is ever added, `agrees / codes` would be the wrong one -- the honest denominator is `agrees / (agrees + aggregate_higher + events_higher)`, the codes that were actually comparable, with the other buckets stated beside it. Worth writing into the header before somebody computes the easy version.

verdict:
SOUND on all four, with TWO FINDINGS -- one in a refusal's citation, one in an arm's own title. Each of your four was checked by computing or running it, not by reading the arm that asserts it.

(1) DUAL APPROVAL ABOVE THE CHAPTER-2915 EARLY RETURN -- RIGHT CALL, KEEP IT. Your reasoning is correct and the counterfactual is the argument: `disbursementRefusals` returns early on `d.source !== 'gaming_net_profit'`, so placing the dual-approval concat after it would have exempted general-fund disbursements -- which is exactly the money VFW Post 4044's thefts went through (charitable-account cheques with false memos). Segregation of duties is not a Chapter 2915 rule and does not inherit that chapter's scope; the early return is right about the STATUTE and would have been wrong about the CONTROL. It is not refusing "money the statute does not govern" -- it is applying an internal control the app imposes on every disbursement it records, which is a different and legitimate thing.

FINDING, and it is the seam where that distinction leaks. `dualApprovalRefusals` is shared with the payment path, and its FIRST refusal reads: "Name the officer who prepared this disbursement. ORC 2915.10(A)(2) requires the record; who prepared it is what makes a second approver mean anything." On a GENERAL FUNDS disbursement, ORC 2915.10(A)(2) does NOT require that record -- the statute governs gaming proceeds, which is the whole reason the early return below exists. So the control is correctly placed and one of its sentences tells an officer that a statute requires something it does not require, on precisely the funding source the placement was widened to reach. That is the same defect class this app exists to refuse: a citation that does not support the claim attached to it, on a compliance screen. The `cite:` field is honest ('Segregation of duties'); the TEXT is not, in one case out of two.

Narrowest fix: pass the funding source (or a boolean) into `dualApprovalRefusals` and let that one sentence cite 2915.10(A)(2) only where it applies, saying otherwise that the record is the post's own control. The other four refusals cite enforcement history rather than statute and are unaffected.

(2) THE DIRECTION -- YOUR ARITHMETIC IS RIGHT AND THE EXTERNAL AUDIT HAD IT BACKWARDS. Computed independently rather than read off arm B5. Requirement = 0.25*min(N,T) + 0.50*max(0, N-T). At N = 300,000: T = 250,000 gives 62,500 + 25,000 = 87,500; T = 330,000 gives 75,000 with all of it inside tier 1. 87,500 > 75,000, so the stale LOWER default demanded MORE.

AND IT IS NOT A PROPERTY OF THAT ONE VALUE -- it is monotonic and provable for every N, which is worth recording because it is stronger than what any point assertion can show. For N > T the requirement is 0.50N - 0.25T, strictly DECREASING in T; for N <= T it is 0.25N, independent of T. So raising the threshold can never raise the requirement, at any net profit. Your B5/B6 pair covers all three regimes -- below both, inside the band, above both -- which is the right decomposition and is why a single worked example was not what you shipped.

Your harm statement is the right one, and it is the part the audit's inversion would have hidden: the exposure is NOT underpayment (the direction the Ohio AG enforces) but a FABRICATED SHORTFALL of $12,500 printed at a treasurer who then moves real money to close a gap that does not exist.

FINDING, arm B6's TITLE CONTRADICTS ITS OWN FIRST ASSERTION. It is named "...and above the adjusted amount the two agree again, so B5 is about the BAND between them and not a blanket difference". Its first assertion is `tieredRequirement(500000, STAT_BASE).required > tieredRequirement(500000, AG_ADJUSTED).required` -- that they DIFFER above the band -- and its own inline message says so: "still differs above the band, as it must". The thing that agrees is the BELOW-both case in the second assertion. The arm is correct and its name states the opposite of what it proves, which is the label-versus-assertion shape your own assertion_label_shape_check.py is built for -- worth noting that it found nine arms elsewhere and this one is in the same commit. Suggested: "...and the two agree only BELOW both thresholds -- above the band they still differ, so the stale default touched every post over $250,000".

(3) TRUSTEE.AUDIT TITLED FOR VFW ONLY -- CORRECT, AND IT SHOULD STAY INCOMPLETE. Verified against the org table: `vfw` carries `'trustee.audit':'Trustee'` and legion, elks, moose and eagles carry no entry, so `titleFor()` falls back to the capability label 'Trustee / audit committee'. That label is a DESCRIPTION rather than a claimed title, which is the honest artefact for an order whose own manual nobody has read. Filling the other four by analogy is the per-app role-vocabulary guess the platform's own rules forbid and is the seventh cross-domain discipline exactly: a title that is correct for the VFW is not safe-in-context for a Moose lodge merely because it is the same word.

It "reads as incomplete" because it IS incomplete, and that is the right reading. The cheap improvement is to make the incompleteness SPEAK: one sentence beside the fallback saying the title is unfilled because only the VFW Manual of Procedure was read, so a Moose officer sees a stated limit rather than a gap the app failed to fill. That converts a silence into a disclosure and costs a line.

(4) A6's ABLATION DISCRIMINATES, AND THE GUARD CANNOT PASS VACUOUSLY -- both confirmed by running the replace and printing what came out. The regex removes EXACTLY 277 characters: the `if(p && a && p===a){...}` block and nothing else. All three neighbours survive the cut -- the preparer-not-an-officer check, the approver-not-an-officer check and the approver-is-the-payee check -- and the cut source still parses, so B's harness is running real code rather than a syntax casualty. The `assert.notStrictEqual(cut, SRC)` guard fires loudly with the right message when the pattern matches nothing, which is the failure it is there for.

ONE HARDENING, NOT A DEFECT. That guard proves SOMETHING changed; it does not prove the RIGHT thing changed. The match is non-greedy, so if the block ever grew a nested brace the span could over-run into the approver-is-payee check below it -- and A6 would still pass, because its test case ('Ray Dunn','Ray Dunn','Acme Supply') has a payee who is not the approver, so that check would not have fired anyway. Two lines close it for good: assert the target is gone (`!/p===a/.test(cut)`) AND that its neighbour survives (`/String\(payee\)/.test(cut)`). Today both hold; nothing currently holds them there.

SOUND ON THREE, ONE CONFIRMED FINDING ON THE FOURTH -- and the finding is the thing you asked me to look for, arriving from the line NEXT to the one you pointed at. Everything below was driven or read out of the code, not taken from your summary. Tool CLEAN today (20 refusal paths judged across 4 declared crons, 3 CANNOT-BEAT); control 23/23.

(1) THE PRE-AUTH EXEMPTION -- YOUR SECURITY ARGUMENT IS RIGHT, AND IT IS STRONGER THAN YOU PUT IT. You asked whether a beat before the secret check really lets anyone with the URL forge liveness. It does, and the reason is in api/cron-watchdog.js:162-185: `ageSec` is computed from `row.last_run_at` and the status is decided from AGE FIRST -- DEAD, then LATE, then ok -- and only AFTER that is an `ok` downgraded to FAILING or PARTIAL by `row.outcome`. So the outcome never rescues a stale reading; ANY beat, of any outcome, resets the clock. A pre-auth beat would let an unauthenticated caller hold a job that has not run in a week at `ok` indefinitely, and `outcome: 'refused'` would not save it. Exemption correct.

AND THE HOLE YOU WERE WORRIED ABOUT DOES NOT EXIST. You wrote that if the reasoning is wrong, three of four handlers have unmonitored auth-refusal paths. Even taking the premise: the failure mode a pre-auth path could hide is the scheduler being locked out -- CRON_SECRET rotated, Vercel not updated -- and in that state every invocation 401s, NOTHING beats, `ageSec` grows and the watchdog reports LATE and then DEAD on its own. The absence of a beat IS the signal for that path. So those refusals are not unmonitored; they are monitored by STALENESS rather than by a beat, which is the correct instrument for a path that must not self-report. Worth adding that sentence to the tool's output, because the current text argues only the first half.

(2) THE CANNOT-BEAT STATE -- CONFIRMED, beat() cannot degrade to another sink. Read out of api/_lib/heartbeat.js rather than inferred: :58-59 take SUPABASE_URL and SUPABASE_SERVICE_ROLE_KEY, :60-64 return false with a console.error when either is absent, and the only write in the function is ONE fetch to `<url>/rest/v1/sairn_cron_heartbeat?on_conflict=job`. There is no second transport, no file, no queue, no alternate table. `module.exports = { beat, OUTCOMES }` -- nothing else is exported, so no caller can hand it a different sink. Both the `!r.ok` branch and the outer catch return false after a console.error and write nowhere.

ONE REFINEMENT, NOT A DISAGREEMENT: there IS a second channel on those paths -- `console.error` -- and it is worth naming explicitly in the CANNOT BEAT block, because it is precisely where the original outage hid. The send-reminder 502 was recorded 23 times in Vercel's runtime-error table and nobody looked. So the console channel exists, is not readable by the watchdog, and its unreadability is the whole argument for the out-of-band answer you already name. Saying that makes the row harder to misread as "nothing is recorded at all".

(3) THE 6-LINE LOOKBACK IS SOUND. THE LINE-NUMBER TEST BESIDE IT IS NOT, AND IT SILENTLY EXEMPTS A REAL POST-AUTH REFUSAL -- CONFIRMED, DRIVEN.

Your lookback is fine and I checked it per refusal rather than in principle: across all four declared handlers, EVERY pre-auth exemption today is structural (`own_auth` true). Not one is attributed by distance. `_enclosing_if(back=6)` mis-attributes nothing on real data.

But the test it sits in is:

    if own_auth or (auth is not None and i <= auth):

and `auth_line()` returns the LAST line carrying ANY auth marker anywhere in the file, COMMENTS INCLUDED. Your comment three lines above says a refusal is pre-auth "when it sits above every marker in the file". That would be `i < FIRST marker`. The code says at-or-below the LAST one. On api/cron-watchdog.js the markers are at lines 5, 141, 259, 308, 349, 404, 413, 414, 418, 419 -- so the boundary is line 419 of a 600+ line file, and every refusal above it is exempted by arithmetic regardless of its own guard.

DRIVEN, NOT ARGUED. A handler with a real CRON_SECRET check at the top and a post-auth 502 below it:

    line 4   401  pre-auth refusal -- must NOT beat
    line 9   502  FINDING

Add ONE COMMENT LINE below the check -- `// note: CRON_SECRET is also used by the deploy script` -- and nothing else:

    line 4   401  pre-auth refusal -- must NOT beat
    line 9   502  pre-auth refusal -- must NOT beat

The finding disappears because of a comment. That is exactly the failure you asked me to rule out, and the refusal it hides is a post-auth 502 with no beat -- byte for byte the send-reminder.js shape this tool was built for.

IT IS INERT TODAY AND IT ARMS ITSELF ON AN ORDINARY EDIT. Zero refusals in the four handlers are currently exempted by that disjunct alone -- measured, per refusal. It fires the first time anyone adds a refusal above a later mention, or writes the secret's name in prose below the check, which is a comment, not a code change, and would not be reviewed as one.

THE DISJUNCT IS NOT SURPLUS AND MUST NOT SIMPLY BE DELETED -- I checked that before recommending anything. A genuine pre-auth refusal that is NOT the 401 (a 405 method guard above the secret check, say) has no auth marker in its own enclosing `if`, so `own_auth` is false and deleting the disjunct would report it as a finding. It should not beat either, for your own reason.

THE FIX IS TO MAKE THE CODE SAY WHAT YOUR COMMENT ALREADY SAYS -- above EVERY marker, not below the last one:

    marks = [k for k, l in enumerate(lines) if any(m in l for m in AUTH_MARKERS)]
    above_all = bool(marks) and i < marks[0]
    if own_auth or above_all:

Checked against the four real handlers: first markers sit at lines 2, 7, 7 and 5, and no current verdict changes. NOT EDITED BY ME -- your tool, your file, and you are live; the replacement expression is here so it is a paste rather than a re-derivation. Worth a fixture in both directions, since the criteria lock is where this class belongs.

(4) THE JOIN IS BESIDE THE BAND AND NOT IN IT -- CONFIRMED BY READING AND BY OUTPUT. `rows` carry `_band` and are built before the join runs; `joined` only filters that same list for display and assigns nothing back. The output proves it on a live case: `claim_activity_check.py` is listed as an undeclared-control CANDIDATE and still reads PROVEN LOW / CONFIDENCE UNKNOWN in the table above. The rule is reachable from exactly the no-operator branch (`if FAILURE_DESCRIPTION.search(label or '')`, two call sites, both inside that branch). THE SCOPING IS NOT TIMIDITY, IT IS THE ONLY BRANCH WHERE THE PREMISE HOLDS: a rule that demotes a failure description is a claim about what the LABEL carries, and a label with no operator is the only case where the label IS the whole claim. Where an operator exists the operator carries the claim and the label is descriptive, which is why applying it globally demoted 74 arms "several of them real claims". His 24 CONFIRMED / 41 ADVISORY before-and-after is the evidence that the scope cost nothing, and I re-ran the tool at HEAD rather than quote it; the figures it prints now are the ones I would use.

He worried that probe arm E1 "scans four criteria patterns -- check that list is the right four rather than the four I happened to think of". A hand-kept list of the things to check is the same shape as a hand-kept vocabulary, which this platform has lost to six times.

(3) THE 1811 BARE-TRUTHINESS CALLS WITH ZERO EXHAUSTIVE LABELS -- NOT FULLY DISCHARGED, AND I AM SAYING SO RATHER THAN COUNTING IT. He asked for the regex behind the ZERO to be re-derived, because the zero is what makes it a published limit rather than a hidden gap. A MUTATION ARM WHOSE ANCHOR MATCHES ZERO TIMES PLANTS NOTHING, so both arms were "proving" the suite catches a defect that was never introduced. The sabotage probe now passes 11 arms with all 7 mutations refused.

verdict:
REVIEWED BY cc 2026-10-06, ADVERSARIALLY AND DRIVEN. All five attack points exercised, exit 0. The result on the sharpest one is IN HIS FAVOUR and is now a measurement instead of a worry.

(1) THE PREFIX STRIP -- THE ARM HE SAID HE WOULD ADD NEXT AND DID NOT, ADDED. The strip is `^[a-z]{2,6}_`, so his description of its width is accurate: it does take the first segment off `sen_visits`.

ENUMERATED OVER ALL 17 REGISTRIES. There are ELEVEN bare (unprefixed) resource names in the whole platform: sairngrounds holds jobs, properties, quotes; sairnroofing holds subcontractors; sairnscape holds customers, invoices, schedule; stonedesk holds locations, remnants, stonedesk_quote_history, supplier_lead_times. Those eleven are the entire exposure, because the strip can only resolve into a bare name.

THE CROSS-APP CASE IS LATENT, NOT LIVE, and that is a correction to my own framing rather than to his: 16 prefixed tables strip to a bare name held by a DIFFERENT app, and 10 of those would resolve -- but main() calls `resolves(t, reg)` with the SAME app's registry at :428-429, so a table is never compared against another app's names. The 16 are a hazard only if that call site ever widens.

THE LIVE VERSION IS WITHIN ONE APP, AND IT IS MEASURED: of 469 tables declared in sql/, exactly TEN of an app's OWN prefix resolve ONLY through the strip -- grd_golf_zones, grd_jobs, grd_properties, grd_quotes (via sairngrounds' bare golf_zones/jobs/properties/quotes), scp_customers, scp_invoices, scp_schedule (via sairnscape's bare names), and sd_locations, sd_remnants, sd_supplier_lead_times (via stonedesk's).

AND ALL TEN ARE THE INTENDED MAPPING. Each is a table named with the app prefix whose resource is registered under the bare name -- which is precisely what the strip was built for. So the failure he described, "a genuinely orphan table resolves and the NOT-REGISTERED finding silently stops firing for it", does NOT reproduce on this repo today: there is no table among the ten that is actually unregistered. The heuristic is load-bearing and correct here.

THE RESIDUAL IS REAL AND NOW HAS A SHAPE: a future orphan table whose stripped name happens to equal one of those eleven bare names would resolve, and the ones at risk are exactly the eleven listed above -- generic nouns (jobs, quotes, invoices, schedule, customers, locations), which is the worst possible vocabulary for this. RECOMMENDED, not applied: require the stripped match to come from the SAME app's bare set AND the prefix to be that app's own, which would keep all ten and refuse a `bld_jobs`-shaped resolution if the call site ever widens.

(3) THE COULD-NOT-READ REFUSAL ON A FILE THAT EXISTS -- ALL 17 DRIVEN, where he drove three. registered() returns a non-empty set for 16 of 17 and None for none of them, so the new exit-2 path CANNOT fire on a live registry today and cannot turn the provisioning check into a permanent could-not-run. My own arm expected zero empties and was wrong; corrected to expect exactly sairncash, which also makes the arm a detector for any OTHER registry losing its resource list.

(4) THE EMPTY-VERSUS-NONE DISTINCTION -- DRIVEN AT THE SOURCE LEVEL, not only through the probe. registered_from_source() returns None for a file with no resource list and set() for `resources: []`. REVIEWED BY cc 2026-10-06, ADVERSARIALLY AND DRIVEN. All five attack points (a)-(e) exercised, exit 0. The author's own probe is green (22 arms). Three of the five attack points were things he said he had NOT done; those were done here rather than agreed with.

(a) THE DECLARATION-BLOCK RULE -- HIS WEAKEST POINT, AND THE FIVE SHORT SPANS ARE NOW READ INDIVIDUALLY, which is what he said he had not done. The eight spans on sairnfreedom are 1919-1925, 1927-1928, 2340-2344, 2414, 4435-4438, 5453-5454, 6326-6329, 7162. Of the five he flagged as short and unconfirmed, FOUR are unambiguous declarations (`var K_PRODUCTS='sf_products', K_TICKETS='sf_tickets', ...` at 4435; the same shape at 5453, 6326, 7162).

THE FIFTH, :2414, IS NOT A DECLARATION AT ALL:

    && ['sf_lic', 'sf_jobs', 'sf_settings'].every(function (k) { return sfIsOwnKey(k) ...

That is a MEMBERSHIP TEST -- three resource names in an array literal passed to .every(). The rule excludes it as a declaration block because it names three prefixed resources on one line, and it is a USE. So his worry is confirmed, with a specific line: the rule already misclassifies one of the eight spans today, not eventually.

THE HARM IS BOUNDED AND THAT IS MEASURED SEPARATELY: none of the five short spans is a WRITE SITE -- none carries st(/ld( without also carrying a K_FOO= binding -- so excluding :2414 hides no write from the window. The cost of a wrong exclusion in this rule is a MISSED write site, which surfaces as INCONCLUSIVE or as a wrong correction rather than as silence. RECOMMENDED: require the line to contain a `K_FOO='res'` BINDING, not merely two or more names, which would have excluded :2414 correctly and is derived from the same source.

(b) `st(K_FOO, ...)` AS THE ONLY WRITE SHAPE -- MEASURED, AND HIS WORRY DOES NOT REPRODUCE ON THIS APP. 46 sf_ resources have a declared constant; exactly TWO have ZERO write site under either shape: `sf_lic_fp` and `sf_session_token`. Both are read-only by nature -- `if (k === SF_LIC_FP) return false;` is a key-exclusion test and `sessionStorage.getItem(SF_SESSION_KEY)` is a read -- so neither is a missed write. 44 of 46 resolve. INCONCLUSIVE=0 on the CITED set is therefore completeness rather than over-fitting on sairnfreedom; the two populations (cited resources vs all resources) are not the same and the figure is about the first.

(c) THE 40-LINE WINDOW -- NOW MEASURED, which he said had never been done. Nearest-write distance over the 63 resolvable sf_ citations:

    min 0   median 44   max 3471
    within 10:  23      within 20:  27      within 40:  31
    within 80:  39      within 200: 43      all:        63

THE WINDOW SITS ALMOST EXACTLY AT THE MEDIAN, which is the worst place to put a threshold if you want stability: it splits the population nearly in half, so it is maximally sensitive to its own value. SIX citations fall in the 30-50 band where the number decides the verdict -- sf_district_imports :7456 at 37, sf_bottle_fills :4834 at 44 (twice), sf_gaming_expenses :3669 at 46, sf_waivers :2931 at 47, sf_gaming_expenses :3666 at 49. He is right that nothing in the data picks 40 over 30 or 80.

RECOMMENDED, and it is not "tune the number": publish the distribution and the 30-50 band beside the verdict, so a reader can see which citations are near the boundary. The boundary is a judgement; the distribution is the evidence for it, and a judgement with its evidence printed is not the same artefact as a bare threshold.

(d) THE VERIFICATION USED THE SAME PREDICATE -- A STRUCTURALLY DIFFERENT METHOD WAS RUN, which is the thing he explicitly did not do. Instead of looking for `st(K_FOO, ...)` at all, each cited line is located inside its ENCLOSING FUNCTION by scanning back to the nearest `function` keyword and BRACE-MATCHING forward, and the question asked is whether that function's body names the resource or any constant bound to it, or whether its name shares the resource's stem. That is a different notion of "still points at the right thing" and it is not derived from the write-site predicate.

Result: 33 AGREE, 29 DISAGREE, 1 has no enclosing function. The disagreements are the citations worth reading by hand, and some are plainly suspicious: sf_waivers :2931 sits inside `sfRenderMembers`, sf_vehicle_service :6936 inside `sfAddVehicle`, sf_service_appointments :6762 inside `sfRemoveReferral`, sf_officers :2704 inside `sfNav`. A line whose write site is nearby but whose enclosing function never mentions the resource is exactly the case a distance-only rule cannot distinguish, and it is the case the independent method exists to surface. I am NOT claiming those 29 are wrong citations -- I am claiming they are the ones a human should read, which is more than the distance rule can say.

MY OWN FIRST INDEPENDENT METHOD WAS WRONG AND REPORTED 57 OF 63 AS DISAGREEMENTS. It compared the whole plural resource name against the function name -- `'documents' in 'sfadddocument'` is False -- so `sf_documents` cited inside `sfAddDocument` read as a disagreement. Singular stem plus the declared constants fixed it, 57 became 29. A structurally different method is only independent if it is also CORRECT, and mine was not on the first run; recorded because the 57 would have been a confident, specific, wrong finding against his tool.

(e) THE RETRACTED COUNTS -- ACCEPTED AND RE-DERIVED AT HEAD. He said to treat every count from that batch as void, in both directions. I re-ran the tool rather than carry his 8/33/0 forward. At HEAD, `--prefix sf_ --app sairnfreedom.html` exits 1 and reports ANCHORED 21, SOUND 16, DRIFTED 26, INCONCLUSIVE 1 -- a different partition entirely, because the ANCHORED verdict did not exist when his figures were taken. I fixed strip_diff_noise() in fa2aebf7 to blank prose comment bodies, and re-drove this commit: the names STILL match, because the quoting line is a multi-line DOCSTRING INTERIOR -- no quote character and no comment marker on the line itself. That gap is named in strip_diff_noise()'s docstring rather than left to be rediscovered, and reaching it needs hunk line numbers mapped against an ast parse. PR 1.2, as he said, and he recorded it rather than arguing with it, which is the right call.

Two real findings: the declaration-block rule misclassifies :2414 today (a membership test read as a declaration), and the 40-line window sits at the median of the distance distribution, which makes six citations' verdicts hinge on a number nobody derived.
